articles.title: Yes, {} + [] = 0. No, JavaScript Isn’t Broken
articles.description: JavaScript is a legendary programming language. Created in the mid-1990s in just 10 days, it was born...
articles.body_html:
JavaScript is a legendary programming language. Created in the mid-1990s in just 10 days, it was born during the browser wars, when Netscape was trying to deliver a fatal blow to Microsoft. As we all know, that didn't exactly work out as planned… Today, some people love JavaScript, others hate it, and some just make fun of it. But the truth is, the modern web simply wouldn't exist without it!

Over the years, JavaScript has gone through countless revolutions. Its capabilities today are almost incomparable to what the language could do back in the 1990s. There's just one tiny problem… Every change to the language has to take into account the fact that millions of websites out there still rely on old JavaScript behavior. And some of those websites will probably continue running that code until the end of time.

So, well, JavaScript's weirdness is probably here to stay forever! 😂

After quite a long break, I've decided to bring back my once-popular JS WTF series. For a very simple reason. I'm on my way back from iJS Munich, and I still have two hours to kill at Frankfurt Airport… (don't ask). Not enough time to write a groundbreaking, deeply technical article. But definitely too much time to just sit here and stare at the wall.

So let's take a look at one of my favorite JavaScript constructions:

{} + [] // 0

Yes, you read that correctly. Under the right circumstances, if we add an empty object to an empty array in JavaScript, we get zero. And it makes perfect sense! 🤡

Wait, what? Why does this happen?

The first thing you need to know is that JavaScript doesn't necessarily interpret {} as an object in this situation! Depending on the context, the JavaScript parser can treat the expression as two completely separate things.

Consider this code at the beginning of a statement in a classic JavaScript script:

{} + []

JavaScript can interpret it like this:

{}    // An empty block of code
+[]   // Unary plus applied to an empty array (what could go wrong?)

That's right. The first {} isn't an object literal at all. It's simply an empty block of code that does absolutely nothing. And the second part? Well, that's where the fun begins.

The magic of type coercion ✨

The expression:

+[]

is a classic example of type coercion, one of the things our wonderful language is famous for.

As you probably know, JavaScript is a dynamically and weakly typed language.

Dynamic typing means that variables aren't permanently tied to one type. You can assign a number to a variable and then replace it with a string, and JavaScript won't complain.

But there's more! JavaScript also performs implicit type conversions, which is one of the reasons it's often described as weakly typed. And sometimes those conversions produce rather… creative results.

Take our unary plus operator:

+[]

Unlike the binary + operator, which can add numbers or concatenate strings, unary plus tries to convert its operand into a numeric value. In this case, it behaves essentially like:

Number([])

Yes, we're trying to convert an array into a number. Because why wouldn't we?

But before JavaScript can complete this operation, it needs to perform another conversion. An array is an object, and JavaScript first needs to obtain a primitive value from it. For an ordinary empty array, that process ends up calling its toString() method.

And guess what?

[].toString(); // ""

An empty array becomes an empty string.

So our conversion effectively looks like this:

Number([]);

// First, the array becomes a primitive string:
Number("");

// Then, the empty string becomes:
0

Because:

Number("") // 0

And therefore:

+[] // 0

Which means our original construction:

{} + []

when parsed as an empty block followed by unary plus, effectively becomes:

{} // Do absolutely nothing

+[] // 0

And that's how we get zero! Simple and obvious, right? 🤡

To be fair, I can't think of another language where exactly this construction would produce such a perfectly normal-looking result. Even our beloved PHP would, I believe, throw a fatal error for something like this. Although PHP has its own collection of fascinating surprises, so perhaps we shouldn't judge too harshly.

One important detail: this behavior depends on how the code is parsed. For example:

// In a classic script, as a standalone statement:
{} + [] // 0

// Force JavaScript to interpret {} as an object:
({} + []) // "[object Object]"

// Inside a function call:
console.log({} + []); // "[object Object]"

Okay, but what about [] + []?

Now that you understand type coercion, this one should be obvious:

[] + [] // ""

Here we're dealing with the binary + operator. JavaScript converts both arrays into primitive values. Well, what else would you expect when adding two empty strings together? 😀 Nothing plus nothing equals nothing! Beautiful.

And now, apparently, addition isn't even commutative 😂

Following the same logic, let's try another expression:

[] + {} // "[object Object]"

Wait a minute.

Didn't we just establish that:

{} + [] // 0

So why does reversing the operands give us something completely different? Apparently, even the commutative property of addition is optional in JavaScript. xD

Well, technically, we're not always performing mathematical addition here, and the parser treats these expressions differently.

But let's not ruin a good joke with technical details. Here's what actually happens. In this expression:

[] + {}

The empty array becomes an empty string:

[].toString() // ""

And the empty object? Well, a regular JavaScript object has its own wonderful string representation:

({}).toString() // "[object Object]"

So JavaScript effectively performs:

"" + "[object Object]"

Which gives us:

"[object Object]"

And that's it! Simple as building a flail. Okay, that's a literal translation of a Polish saying, proste jak budowa cepa, which means something is ridiculously easy to understand. And I think it fits JavaScript perfectly. 😂

Final thoughts

I hope you enjoyed this little journey into the wonderful world of JavaScript weirdness. And I hope that after reading this article, you'll appreciate the beauty and originality of this magnificent language even more.

After all, JavaScript has been keeping us entertained for over 30 years, and I strongly suspect it has plenty of surprises left.

And the best part? None of the examples above are bugs. They're all consequences of JavaScript's parsing rules, type coercion, and the language's long history of backward compatibility. So next time someone tells you JavaScript is broken because {} + [] can equal 0, you can proudly explain why it makes perfect sense.

Next time I'll tell you why {} + {} = NaN... but unfortunately time flies when you're having fun, and I'll have to get ready for my flight soon!

P.S. If you enjoy my content, feel free to connect with me or leave a like on LinkedIn! ❤️

articles.title: We Need to Talk About How Gross Modern Web Design Has Become (And How We Built an AI to Catch It)
articles.description: Let me paint a picture I know you’ve experienced recently.  You’re trying to book a flight, buy...
articles.body_html:
Let me paint a picture I know you’ve experienced recently.

You’re trying to book a flight, buy concert tickets, or just download a simple PDF converter. Suddenly, the website turns into an absolute warzone:

🚨 "ONLY 2 SEATS LEFT AT THIS PRICE!"
⏳ A blood-red countdown timer ticks down from 05:00.
🟢 Three massive, glowing "DOWNLOAD NOW" buttons appear, and you know two of them will install malware.
🥺 And when you try to close the popup? The only button says, "No thanks, I'd rather pay full price and be miserable."

We call this "marketing." But let’s be honest: it’s just deceptive engineering.

These are Dark Patterns—UI/UX choices intentionally designed to trick, guilt, or force you into doing things you didn't want to do. And honestly? It’s getting gross. As developers, we build the web. We shouldn't be okay with the web actively manipulating its users.

So, my team at Tarkash Labs decided to fight back. We built a cognitive visual shield to catch these patterns in real-time.

Meet OmniGuard AI.


(Watch the 1-minute demo above to see it catch fake timers and hidden fees live!)

🛡️ How OmniGuard Works (The Tech Stack)

The problem with most ad-blockers or privacy extensions is that they rely on static blocklists or CSS selectors. But modern dark patterns are dynamic. They are disguised as regular DOM elements.

To catch them, we needed a tool that could see the web exactly how a human sees it.

We built OmniGuard as a Manifest V3 Chrome Extension powered by a FastAPI backend and Gemini 3.7 Flash.

Here is the exact flow:

1. The "Eyes" (React 18 + Vite Extension):
When you click "Scan" (or enable auto-scan on scroll), the extension captures an ephemeral, highly compressed screenshot of your active viewport.

2. The "Brain" (FastAPI + Gemini 3.7 Flash):
The image is sent to our stateless FastAPI backend. We use Gemini 3.7 Flash’s multimodal capabilities to analyze the visual context of the page. It doesn't just read the code; it understands how the UI looks.

3. The "Shield" (Shadow DOM Injection):
If Gemini detects a dark pattern, the backend streams the exact coordinates back to the extension. We then inject a Shadow DOM layer over the page, drawing glowing red bounding boxes precisely over the deceptive elements—completely isolating our CSS from the host page's styles.

🕵️‍♂️ The 6 Villains We Hunt

OmniGuard is currently configured to detect six specific categories of visual deception. Here is how it catches them in the wild:

1. Disguised Clicks
Buttons masquerading as something else (like fake downloads that lead to ads or malware).

2. Confirmshaming
Guilt-loaded opt-out language designed to make you feel bad for not subscribing.

3. Urgency Traps
Fake countdowns and artificial scarcity messages.

4. Hidden Costs (Drip Pricing)
Fees and excluded taxes that magically appear at the very end of a checkout journey.

5. Sneak into Basket
Unwanted software bundles or insurances silently pre-checked during a download or checkout.

6. Forced Continuity
"Free trials" that hide their aggressive auto-renewal terms in the fine print.

🔒 Zero-DB Privacy Architecture

One of the biggest challenges of building an AI extension that takes screenshots of your browser is privacy. We knew from day one that if we were building a tool to protect users, we couldn't compromise their data to do it.

That’s why the OmniGuard backend is 100% stateless. It uses a zero-DB architecture. The viewport screenshot exists only in memory for the milliseconds it takes Gemini to process it, and is then immediately destroyed. Nothing is ever saved, logged, or stored.

💻 Try It Yourself (Open Source)

We’ve open-sourced the entire project. If you want to see how we handled Manifest V3 tab capturing, or how we prompted Gemini Flash for UI coordinate mapping, you can check out the repo here:

Tarkash-Labs / OmniGuard

OmniGuard is a real-time, multimodal browser extension acting as a cognitive visual shield against deceptive UI/UX. Powered by Gemini , it instantly detects "Dark Patterns"—like fake timers or hidden costs—and injects HTML5 Canvas bounding boxes to protect users before they click. Built on a secure, zero-DB privacy architecture.

🛡️ OmniGuard AI

Real-Time Multimodal Dark Pattern & Visual Deception Radar

OmniGuard AI is a Chrome browser extension that acts as a cognitive visual shield against deceptive UI/UX. Powered by Gemini 3.7 Flash, it captures what users actually see on a webpage, detects dark patterns in real-time, and overlays live bounding boxes directly on the deceptive elements — before users can click.

Built by Tarkash Labs

✨ Features

OmniGuard detects 6 categories of dark patterns in real-time:

Category Description Example
⏰ Urgency Traps Fake countdowns & artificial scarcity "Only 2 left! Order in 03:22!"
🎭 Disguised Clicks Buttons masquerading as something else Fake download buttons, hidden ads
🛒 Sneak into Basket Unwanted items silently added Pre-checked insurance add-ons
🔄 Forced Continuity Subscription traps & hidden renewals Free trial → auto-charge
😢 Confirmshaming Guilt-loaded opt-out language "No thanks, I hate saving money"
💰 Hidden Costs Fees revealed late in the
…

Massive shoutout to my teammates Yug Vasava (Lead Dev) and Avadh Vaishnani (Lead QA) for helping bring this to life.

👇 Now, I need to know...

We are constantly trying to improve the AI's detection capabilities.

What is the most unethical, infuriating, or downright gross dark pattern you’ve seen a company use recently?

Drop it in the comments below so we can train OmniGuard to catch it! 🚀

articles.title: 💀I'm the last mail carrier in the land of the dead. An open-weight model writes all the mail.
articles.description: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Week 4: Ghost in the...
articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Week 4: Ghost in the Machine.

ÁNIMAS is a small 3D browser game set in Mictlán, the land of the dead, on Día de los Muertos. You play a skeleton mail carrier who helps lost ghosts cross over by delivering their letters and finding the things they miss.

Every ghost in the game (name, backstory, personality, dialogue, the item they miss) and every letter between ghosts is written by Gemma 4, an open-weight model, using structured JSON output. The game ships with 24 pre-generated ghosts so it plays instantly in any browser, and it can connect to a Gemma server to write new ones live while you play.

What I Built

Play ÁNIMAS in your browser

You play a little calaca, a skeleton in a striped serape with a crown of marigolds: the last mail carrier of Mictlán, the Aztec land of the dead, on the one night of the year when the souls go home. The ghosts wandering the town have unfinished business. Some want a letter carried to another ghost. Some miss one small thing (a guitar, a pocket watch, a cup of chocolate) that's waiting somewhere in the world. Deliver it, and they cross over.

The town is meant to be wandered:

  • Four barrios of pastel houses around a plaza with a great ofrenda. Every roof is walkable. You climb outside stairs, stacked crates and market awnings, then cross planks from rooftop to rooftop.
  • A chapel whose bell tower you climb flight by flight. A hillside of terraces that ends in a lookout and a long, high plank out to La Campana, a floating rock with a bell.
  • Rope bridges to the islands around town: a cemetery, a floating market, an orchard, a dock with stepping stones across the water to a tiny islet, and a staircase of floating stones up to El Mirador, the highest point in the world.
  • Three houses you can walk into: a grandmother's house with a stove and a little ofrenda, a watchmaker's workshop, the blue house. Each has a staircase up to a hatch in the roof, and something someone is missing waiting inside.
  • Golden calaveras hidden on rooftops, towers, awnings and the far ends of things. The game never tells you where they are.
  • A minimap that turns with your camera, a full map (M), and a mail bag that holds up to four deliveries at once, so you can plan a route.

And then there are the wings 🪽 Free three souls and they give you wings (Alas de papel): in the air, tap Space to beat them, hold it to glide. Six souls, and they fill with marigolds and carry you further. Ten, and you become el Ángel de Mictlán, with a halo and a trail of light, flying over the rooftops you used to climb. Some golden calaveras are only reachable by wing, including one on La Nube, a cloud island high above the town. You'll know what you're working towards: a few other (NPC) mail carriers make their rounds through the streets, and the ones who already earned their wings glide over the rooftops above you.

Demo

🔗 Live:

🎃 ÁNIMAS 👻

🪽 ÁNIMAS is a small 3D browser game set in Mictlán, on Día de los Muertos.

Live Demo 🔥 - https://animas-virid.vercel.app

The hosted version plays with the ghosts and letters Gemma wrote ahead of time; run the repo locally to have Gemma keep writing new ones.

🎮 Play it now:

A few other letters waiting in the mail tonight, all written by Gemma 4 E2B on a 2-core CPU with no GPU:

Dolores → Mateo · neighbors who shared sweet bread on the same street
"Do you remember how we tried to bake that disastrous sourdough last summer? It ended up looking like a melted swamp, but we laughed until our bellies hurt."
Mateo: "Oh, the swamp! I still chuckle thinking about that."

Nonna Pina → Ama · they shared stories of mythical creatures
"I remember the night we huddled under the old mango tree, and you told me the secret names of the forest spirits."

Benedita → Felipe · a love for forgotten folk songs
"Remember the night we thought the moon was actually a giant, silver cat?"
Felipe: "That tune… I haven't heard that melody in fifty years."

Controls: move the mouse to look (click the world once), WASD walks wherever you're looking · Shift run · Space jump (twice for a flip; with wings, again to flap, hold to glide) · E talk · 1/2/3 choose · M map · Tab next delivery · F dance. On a phone: a thumbstick on the left, drag the right side to look, buttons for jump, talk and dance.

When the game runs with its keeper server (npm start + Gemma), you can also summon someone you miss at the great ofrenda. Describe them in a sentence and Gemma turns them into a ghost who wanders the town tonight, for strangers to meet. It's the only place in the game where you type, and your words are never stored, only the ghost.

How I Built It

Code: github.com/longphanquangminh/animas (MIT).

longphanquangminh / animas

🪽 ÁNIMAS is a small 3D browser game set in Mictlán, on Día de los Muertos.

💀 ÁNIMAS

The last mail carrier in the land of the dead. Every ghost, and every letter they send each other, is written by an open-weight model.

A 3D exploration game for Día de los Muertos. You are a small calaca in a striped serape and a crown of marigolds, walking the town of Mictlán on the one night the souls go home. Ghosts wander its plaza, rooftops and outer islands. Some want a letter carried to another ghost; some miss one small thing waiting somewhere in the world. Deliver it, and they cross over, rising into a sky of lanterns that everyone online shares.

Every ghost and every letter is written by Gemma 4, running on your own machine or server, under JSON-Schema grammars.

Built for the DEV Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 4: Ghost in the Machine.
