…
View on GitHub

There's no game engine, no build step and no 3D model files. The client is Three.js with hand-written shaders. The server is plain Node with zero npm dependencies. Gemma 4 runs behind Ollama or llama.cpp.

Two grammars: one for people, one for mail

The keeper (that's what the server calls the model) doesn't get asked nicely for JSON. It gets a grammar. The server sends a JSON Schema, the runtime compiles it into a grammar, and at every decoding step any token that would break the schema gets a probability of zero.

Ghosts have a name, a hometown, a life, a personality, a greeting, a memory, the object they miss, an ask, a thank-you and an epitaph. The object is an enum of twelve things that physically exist on pedestals around the world, so every errand Gemma invents is solvable.

Letters are written later, between two ghosts that are both wandering right now. The server picks a sender and a recipient, hands Gemma both of their lives, and asks it to invent the connection:

const LETTER_SCHEMA = {
  type: "object",
  properties: {
    relation: { type: "string", maxLength: 70 },   // "neighbors who shared sweet bread on the same street"
    ask:      { type: "string", maxLength: 170 },  // the sender asks you to carry it
    letter:   { type: "string", pattern: "^Dear [^,]{1,30}, .{60,400}$" },
    reply:    { type: "string", maxLength: 200 },  // the recipient, out loud, after reading
  },
  required: ["relation", "ask", "letter", "reply"],
};

That pattern is there because of a lesson. In my first batch, about half the "letters" came back as descriptions of letters: "From Kofi to Sal, referencing shared memories (film/ramen)." The model understood the task and summarized it instead of doing it. A one-line example in the prompt, plus a grammar that forces the field to literally start with Dear <name>,, fixed it. Every letter since has been a real letter.

The same thing happened with objects. When Gemma could pick any of the twelve, 9 of 24 ghosts chose the marigold crown, and then asked in their dialogue for a spoon or a fountain pen. The structured field was perfect; the prose wandered off. Now the server rolls dice (name, place, decade, job, personality, soul color, and an object that follows from the job: a baker misses pan dulce, a clockmaker a pocket watch) and builds a grammar for that one ghost, with the object pinned as a single-value enum placed first, before any prose. The grammar guarantees the shape. The dice guarantee the meaning.

Gemma 4 and the empty thought channel

Gemma 4 can think before it answers, inside a special thought channel. On llama.cpp the grammar is relaxed inside that channel, so the model sometimes rambled there and never came back to the JSON. The fix: I render the chat template myself and append an empty thought channel (<|channel>thought\n<channel|>) before generation starts, so the grammar governs every token from the first one. (On Ollama, think: false does the same job.) That's only possible when you control the prompt down to its special tokens.

Writing ahead of the player

On the box where I built this, Gemma 4 E2B takes about a minute to write a ghost and 15 to 60 seconds to write a letter. Nobody waits for it. The server keeps a pool of ghosts written ahead of time, and a second loop keeps about half of the wandering ghosts holding a letter for another wandering ghost. When a letter's recipient crosses over before you arrive, there's a red mailbox by the Correo that sends it to the other side. The model works like a novelist in the back room, not a chatbot at the counter.

A town you can climb

The town is generated in code from a fixed seed, so every player gets the same streets. Collision is three small ideas:

  • pads: round islands whose cliffs are walls,
  • boxes: houses, crates, awnings, the tower (a walkable top and solid sides),
  • ramps: stairs, planks and rope bridges (walkable, no walls).

The character controller steps up anything under 0.8 m, jumps about 2 m (3.5 m with the double jump), and has coyote time. Fall into the river and it carries you back to the last shore you stood on. The camera pulls in when a house gets between it and you.

To make sure the town is fair, I wrote a reachability check: a breadth-first search over the whole map using the same rules as the character (step up 0.8 m, jump up to about 3 m, drop any distance). It runs in a headless browser and reports anything that can't be reached from the plaza. The first run found that the stepping stones to the islet and to El Mirador were a little too far apart. Now every calavera, every object and every ghost passes.

A skeleton made of code

There are no model files in the repo. The calaca is a few dozen primitives: a sugar-skull face painted onto a canvas texture, glowing pupils that blink, bone limbs on pivots, a serape whose stripes come from the player's hue, a crown of flowers. Walking, running, jumping, the mid-air flip, carrying an object overhead, gesturing while talking and dancing (F, try it) are procedural animation with squash and stretch. Ghosts are a lathe-turned sheet with a shader: a glow in their soul's color, a rippling hem, and a mouth that moves while their words type out in Animal-Crossing-style babble, at a pitch derived from their name.

Around them: thousands of instanced marigolds and candles, papel picado on sagging ropes, glowing windows, a mirror-water river, drifting marigold wisps, souls rising slowly while petals fall, monarch butterflies (said to be the returning souls), bloom and film grain. All the sound is procedural Web Audio.

Why open innovation matters here

I needed control below the API. Compiling my own schemas into grammars, pinning the object per ghost, forcing a letter to begin with "Dear", appending an empty thought channel token by token: none of that is available through a closed chat API, and the game design depends on all of it.

A town that writes its own mail needs an AI that costs electricity, not tokens. The server writes ghosts and letters in the background forever. With a per-token bill I'd ration them. With open weights on my own box, the mail never stops.

Some of these ghosts are real people. When someone summons a grandparent at the ofrenda, those words are grief. They don't belong in a third-party provider's logs. With an open model, the memory goes from the browser to a server I control, becomes a ghost, and the original words are thrown away.

A memorial shouldn't disappear when an API does. Open weights on disk and a dependency-free server will still run in 2036, and anyone can host a Mictlán for their own family.

Come pick up the mail

Play ÁNIMAS. Deliver a few letters, earn your wings, then tell me in the comments who wrote to whom and how many golden calaveras you found. (There's one on top of the bell tower, and one even higher. That's all I'm saying.)

They're not gone while someone still remembers. 🌼💀✉️

Prize categories: Best Use of Gemma. Gemma 4 writes every ghost and every letter in the game, under JSON-Schema grammars that keep every errand solvable and every letter a real letter.

Solo submission by @longphanquangminh.

articles.title: Sig.js Has Reached Version 1.0
articles.description: Well, we did it.  Sig.js is officially at version 1.0 and available on npm.  And I have to admit,...
articles.body_html:
Well, we did it.

Sig.js is officially at version 1.0 and available on npm.

And I have to admit, this one feels pretty good.

I've spent a lot of time writing about KiwiEngine, its architecture, its individual libraries, and the philosophy behind building a system from smaller, focused components.

I've talked about why I want to build an engine instead of another collection of loosely connected utilities.

I've talked about intentional programming, abstractions, responsibility, and giving developers more control without making them rebuild everything.

But eventually, all that thinking has to turn into something.

Something that works.

Something that can be installed.

Something that other developers can actually use.

Today, Sig.js crossed that milestone.

From An Idea To A Published Library

For anyone who hasn't been following the series, Sig.js is the reactive UI library I've been developing as part of KiwiEngine.

It's built around signals and a lightweight JSX rendering model.

The goal is to make reactive interfaces understandable without requiring an enormous framework around them.

At its core, I wanted something that could answer a fairly straightforward question:

When application state changes, how does the interface respond?

That sounds simple.

And conceptually, it is.

But once you start building a reactive rendering system, the questions get considerably more interesting.

How are dependencies tracked?

How do effects respond to changes?

How do components manage their lifecycle?

What happens when something gets removed from the interface?

How should rendering and cleanup work together?

How do you prevent the abstraction from becoming more complicated than the problem?

Those are the kinds of questions that shaped Sig.

Sig Is More Than A Signals Utility

One of the important developments along the way was establishing Sig as more than a small reactive state library.

Signals are the foundation.

But the library also provides the machinery needed to build interfaces around them.

That includes:

  • Reactive signals and effects
  • Derived values through memoization
  • A JSX runtime
  • Component mounting and cleanup
  • Reactive DOM behavior
  • A lightweight router
  • Integration with Juice

These pieces give Sig a much clearer identity.

It's not trying to become an entire application framework.

It's becoming a focused reactive UI engine.

And that distinction matters.

The JSX Runtime Was A Big Step

I wanted KiwiEngine to have a way to describe interactive interfaces without requiring another framework to own the rendering model.

JSX gives me an expressive way to describe the interface.

Sig handles the reactive behavior underneath it.

That's a useful separation.

The syntax describes what should appear.

The reactive system determines how the interface responds to changing state.

The renderer handles the relationship with the DOM.

And lifecycle behavior makes sure the system can clean up after itself.

That last part is especially important.

It's relatively easy to make a counter update.

It's considerably harder to make an entire application behave predictably as components appear, disappear, and change.

That's where the real engineering starts.

The Relationship With Juice Is Becoming Real

Another part of this release that I'm excited about is the integration with Juice.

I've written quite a bit about Juice recently.

Juice is becoming the design and styling engine within KiwiEngine.

It translates design intent and configuration into styling behavior.

Sig handles reactivity.

Those are different responsibilities.

But interfaces need both.

A checkbox might have a visual state.

A disclosure might open or close.

A modal might become visible.

An interactive control might need to communicate its state back to the application.

The Sig and Juice integration creates a way for those systems to work together without turning them into one enormous library.

And importantly, that integration is optional.

Sig doesn't have to become Juice.

Juice doesn't have to become Sig.

They can remain independent systems that become more capable when composed.

That's exactly the architecture I've been trying to build.

Getting To Version 1 Wasn't About Adding Everything

This is probably the biggest lesson of the release.

There are still things Sig doesn't do.

There are still things I want to explore.

There are still experimental APIs.

And there are capabilities that I've deliberately decided don't belong in this first stable release.

For example, server-side rendering isn't part of Sig 1.0.

Neither is a virtual DOM.

I'm not trying to reproduce every abstraction available in other UI frameworks.

I'm trying to establish a focused model that makes sense for Sig.

Some capabilities may arrive later.

Some may never belong.

And that's okay.

A library doesn't become mature simply because it has more features.

Sometimes maturity means becoming more comfortable with its limitations.

Version 1 Is A Commitment

I've said this before in the series, but I think it's worth repeating.

Version 1.0 doesn't mean a library is finished.

It means something closer to:

I understand what this library is, and I'm ready to establish a dependable foundation around that understanding.

For Sig, that means the stable public API now carries a stronger compatibility commitment.

Changes need to be more deliberate.

Breaking existing behavior has consequences.

Documentation becomes more important.

Testing becomes more important.

The developer experience becomes more important.

It's no longer just a collection of experiments I can freely reshape whenever another idea comes along.

It's a library with a public contract.

And that's a different kind of responsibility.

The Release Was About Stabilizing, Not Reinventing

Something I particularly like about this milestone is that version 1.0 didn't require inventing a completely new API.

The release formalizes the API developed through the previous 0.7.x work.

That's how I want these libraries to mature.

Experiment.

Build.

Test.

Refine.

Use the library.

Discover where the abstraction is awkward.

Improve it.

Then, when the design becomes stable enough, establish that contract.

I don't want version numbers to become a marketing exercise.

I want them to mean something.

Testing Outside The Monorepo Matters

There's another important part of releasing a library that can be easy to overlook.

It's one thing for a package to work inside the repository where it was developed.

It's another thing for someone to install it from npm into an independent project.

That distinction matters.

A library shouldn't require mysterious workspace configuration or internal repository knowledge just to get started.

For this release, the standalone counter example was tested against the published npm package.

That included installation, TypeScript checking, and building the application.

It's a small example.

But it proves something important.

Sig isn't just a piece of the KiwiEngine repository.

It can exist as a published package that developers install and use.

That's a meaningful step toward the kind of modular ecosystem I want.

You Can Install Sig.js Now

Sig.js 1.0 is published under the CitrusWorx npm scope.

npm install @citrusworx/sigjs

The package includes its reactive core, JSX runtime, router, and optional Juice integration.

You don't need to adopt all of KiwiEngine just to explore Sig.

That's intentional.

I've always wanted the individual libraries to have their own identities and responsibilities.

They should be useful within the larger ecosystem.

But they shouldn't exist only because the larger ecosystem exists.

This Is A Milestone For KiwiEngine Too

This is the part that makes the release especially exciting to me.

Sig reaching 1.0 isn't just a milestone for Sig.

It's progress toward KiwiEngine becoming the engine I've been describing throughout this series.

Because an engine needs dependable components.

Not just promising prototypes.

Not just architectural diagrams.

Not just ideas about how everything might work together someday.

It needs actual systems with defined responsibilities and stable interfaces.

Juice is continuing toward that point.

Nectarine is developing its role.

Seltzer is establishing its communication boundaries.

WebEngine is bringing the pieces together.

And now Sig has reached its first stable major release.

One of the components is ready to stand on its own.

That's real progress.

Now I Get To Build With It

This is probably what I'm looking forward to most.

I've spent a lot of time building tools for building things.

And I enjoy that.

I genuinely enjoy architecture.

I enjoy thinking about APIs.

I enjoy designing systems.

But I also have a lot of applications I want to create.

Blackwater Sound.

WebStore.

Artist platforms.

Music software.

Interactive creative tools.

Applications that support my other businesses and projects.

Sig is part of the foundation that will help me build those things.

And now I have a stable release I can begin depending on.

That's the payoff.

Not the version number by itself.

What the version number allows me to start doing.

The Road Doesn't End At 1.0

There's still plenty of work ahead.

Sig will continue evolving.

There will be bugs to fix.

Documentation to improve.

Patterns to discover through real applications.

And probably a few architectural assumptions that real-world usage will challenge.

That's part of building software.

But the nature of the work is changing.

I'm no longer only trying to figure out what Sig should become.

I'm beginning to build on what it already is.

And that feels like a pretty significant milestone.

Sig.js 1.0 is here.

One library has reached a stable foundation.

One more piece of KiwiEngine is ready.

And the engine is getting closer to doing what I built it for in the first place.

Helping me build the things I've been imagining.

articles.title: Neon Realtime vs Supabase Realtime
articles.description: Neon shipped Realtime on October 15, 2026. You subscribe to a SQL query, and Neon keeps the result up...
articles.body_html:
Neon shipped Realtime on October 15, 2026. You subscribe to a SQL query, and Neon keeps the result up to date as the data changes. Neon hasn't published latency numbers yet, so I measured it.

I compared it with polling, LISTEN/NOTIFY, and both flavors of Supabase Realtime, on 10,000 and 1,000,000 rows. Everything ran on October 28, 2026 in Frankfurt.

TL;DR

Median time from UPDATE to an up-to-date result on the client, at 10k and 1M rows:

  • Neon Realtime: 40–46 ms for filters, joins and top-10 queries. That's one network round trip from my laptop. The change usually arrived within 8 ms of the write's commit ack.
  • Supabase Broadcast: 58–60 ms on a plain filter. Joins and top-10 need a refetch, so 108–115 ms.
  • LISTEN/NOTIFY: 70–244 ms. Every change costs a second query.
  • Supabase Postgres Changes: 328–434 ms, and 1.1 s for the aggregate at 1M rows.
  • Polling every second: 414–546 ms, change or not.
  • The large aggregate used more bandwidth. At 1M rows, Neon still had the lowest latency at 179 ms, but re-sent the full 1,000-group result: ~111 KB per change.
  • Scale-to-zero still works. The compute suspended with a subscription open and stayed suspended for the 10 minutes I watched. The subscription stayed live and got the next write.

What Neon Realtime does

Your server defines the query and seals it into a token that expires after 60 seconds. The browser subscribes with that token over a WebSocket. Neon sends the full result once, then only the changes.

// Server: the query and its parameters stay on your side
import { createRealtime, rawSql } from "@neon/realtime/server";

const realtime = createRealtime({ secret: process.env.NEON_REALTIME_SECRET, db: "neondb" });
const sealed = await realtime.seal({
  query: rawSql("SELECT id, name, score FROM players WHERE team_id = $1", [teamId]),
});
// send `sealed` to the browser

// Browser
import { createRealtimeClient } from "@neon/realtime/client";

const client = createRealtimeClient({ url: NEON_REALTIME_URL });
const subscription = client.subscribe(sealed);
subscription.onChange(({ data }) => render(data));

The client asks your server for a fresh token before the old one expires. The React bindings and QueryRefreshController do that for you.

Limits in the beta:

  • Queries: read-only and deterministic, so no now() or gen_random_uuid(). Joins, aggregates, ORDER BY … LIMIT, subqueries and window functions are supported.
  • Tables: every table needs a primary key.
  • Auth: no row-level security yet. You authorize when you seal the query.
  • Regions: four AWS regions (us-east-1, us-east-2, eu-central-1, ap-southeast-1).
  • Price: Realtime is free during the beta. Compute and egress are billed as usual.

The setup

  • Neon: 0.25 CU (1 GB RAM), Postgres 18.6, aws-eu-central-1.
  • Supabase: Nano instance (0.5 GB RAM, shared CPU), Postgres 17.11, eu-central-1.
  • Client: my laptop, about 40 ms round trip from Frankfurt. That round trip is the floor for every number below.

Both are the smallest compute on their platform. The Supabase project was on the Free plan. The Neon project sat in my Launch-plan org, but Neon's Free plan runs the same 0.25 CU with the same 5-minute scale-to-zero, and the whole benchmark used 0.43 CU-hours of the 100 a month it includes.

The Postgres versions were the defaults. Neon created the project on Postgres 18. Hosted Supabase tops out at 17.11 as of this writing.

The table is players(id, name, team_id, score) with 1,000 teams. Each write is UPDATE players SET score = $1 WHERE id = 1 over an open direct connection. Then I timed how long the subscriber took to see the new score.

Five ways to keep a query live:

  1. Neon Realtime: subscribe to the SQL query.
  2. Supabase Broadcast: a trigger calls realtime.broadcast_changes() into a private channel. Supabase recommends it "for scalability and security".
  3. LISTEN/NOTIFY on Neon: a trigger sends NOTIFY, and the app re-runs the query.
  4. Supabase Postgres Changes: subscribe to row changes on players.
  5. Polling on Neon: re-run the query every second.

The four queries:

  • Filter: the players in one team. 10 rows at 10k, 1,000 rows at 1M.
  • Join: the same players joined with teams.
  • Aggregate: player count and top score for every team (1,000 groups).
  • Top 10: the 10 highest scores across all players.

With both Supabase methods, the client applies the changed row itself for the filter. A change event alone can't update a join, an aggregate or a top 10, so for those the client refetches the query over the REST API.

How I measured
  • One Node process runs the writer and the subscriber, so both timestamps come from the same clock.
  • Write to screen is the time from sending the UPDATE until the subscriber's copy of the result contains the new score. It includes any refetch the method needs.
  • 5 warm-up writes, then 100 writes per cell with a random 250–750 ms gap. Timeout 10 s. Nothing timed out.
  • The Supabase refetches query views through supabase-js, with RLS on and a public read policy.
  • Bytes per change are the WebSocket bytes received plus the size of any refetched result.
  • One writer, one subscriber. I didn't test fan-out to many subscribers.

Write to screen

The differences come down to how many trips a change takes to reach the screen:

  • Neon Realtime: the change arrived between 2 ms before and 8 ms after the writer got its commit ack. So it's as fast as the network allows. The exception is the aggregate at 1M rows (next section).
  • LISTEN/NOTIFY: the notification arrives about as fast as Realtime, then the query runs a second time. At 1M rows the filter returns 1,000 rows (64 KB), so it climbs to 159 ms.
  • Supabase Broadcast: the event arrived ~57 ms after the write in every cell. The REST refetch added 50–70 ms, and ~740 ms for the aggregate at 1M rows.
  • Supabase Postgres Changes: the event alone took 315–384 ms. Supabase's docs say it processes changes on a single thread and checks RLS for every subscriber, and that it "does not scale as well" as Broadcast.
  • Polling: on average you wait half the interval, plus the query. It also runs 86,400 queries a day per client, even when nothing changes.

Getting the first result after subscribing took 0.4–0.8 s on Neon Realtime and 0.8–1.4 s on Supabase Broadcast, including the WebSocket handshake.

At 1–2 writes a second, the write itself took ~40 ms with every method. A live query didn't slow down the writer.

p50 / p95 tables (ms)
10,000 rows
Method Filter Join Aggregate Top 10
Neon Realtime 40 / 56 40 / 48 44 / 51 42 / 123
Supabase Broadcast 58 / 62 110 / 122 125 / 196 108 / 125
LISTEN/NOTIFY 84 / 90 83 / 87 128 / 207 85 / 315
Supabase Postgres Changes 371 / 569 397 / 619 418 / 642 368 / 615
Polling every 1 s 484 / 724 534 / 731 546 / 700 498 / 708

1,000,000 rows

Method Filter Join Aggregate Top 10
Neon Realtime 44 / 52 41 / 54 179 / 191 46 / 74
Supabase Broadcast 60 / 249 115 / 132 793 / 856 110 / 121
LISTEN/NOTIFY 159 / 176 145 / 155 244 / 269 70 / 74
Supabase Postgres Changes 328 / 540 418 / 626 1129 / 1293 434 / 633
Polling every 1 s 542 / 723 495 / 740 517 / 732 414 / 709

Bytes per change

For filters and joins, Neon sends only the changed row, ~0.4 KB per change, whatever the table size. A refetch downloads the whole result again: 64–73 KB per change at 1M rows.

The large aggregate exposes Neon's bandwidth tradeoff. At 10k rows, each change arrived as a ~0.4 KB delta. At 1M rows the engine switched to re-sending the full 1,000-group result: ~111 KB and 179 ms per change. That's more than twice the data transferred by a refetch. Neon's docs warn that "complex queries add write-processing latency, especially on larger datasets."

Top 10 re-sends the full result on every change too, but that's only 1.8 KB.

Supabase's aggregate refetch took ~740 ms after the event at 1M rows. Part of that is the Nano instance: the same query took ~200 ms on Neon's 0.25 CU. Bigger Supabase compute would help.

Scale to zero

Neon suspends a compute after 5 minutes without queries. I opened a Realtime subscription while the compute was suspended, then left it alone (twice). For comparison, I did the same with a plain LISTEN connection.

  • The subscription woke the compute: first result in 1.3–2.5 s.
  • The compute suspended anyway, 5.3–5.4 minutes later, with the subscription open.
  • It stayed suspended. In the second run I watched for 10 more minutes. The compute never woke, though the subscription's token renewed every minute.
  • The subscription stayed live. A write to the sleeping database woke it (ack in 917–965 ms, most of it connecting), and the subscriber had the change 9–48 ms after the ack.
  • LISTEN didn't block suspension either, but Neon terminated the connection after 5 min 18 s (57P01). The registration is gone, notifications sent before you reconnect are lost, and reconnecting wakes the compute again.

So an open dashboard tab doesn't keep the database billing. Polling does, because it never stops querying.

Caveats

  • One subscriber and one writer at 1–2 writes a second. Fan-out and heavy write load are untested.
  • Every number includes a ~40 ms round trip from my laptop. A server in the same region would see lower numbers everywhere.
  • Supabase's Nano has half the RAM of Neon's 0.25 CU and a shared CPU. That affects refetch-heavy cells, not event delivery.
  • Neon Realtime is a beta. Neon says the protocol isn't stable yet.
  • One run per configuration, on one day.

Which one should you use?

  • Neon Realtime: live results of real queries (lists, joins, leaderboards, per-user views) on Neon. Watch large aggregates, and authorize at seal time until RLS lands.
  • Supabase Broadcast: you're on Supabase and the client can apply the changed row itself.
  • LISTEN/NOTIFY: any Postgres, a small result, and you're fine with a refetch per change. On Neon, reconnect after the compute suspends.
  • Supabase Postgres Changes: prototypes. Supabase itself points you to Broadcast.
  • Polling: when a few seconds of delay is fine and the database is awake anyway.

Sources

Checked October 28, 2026.

  • Neon: Realtime launch, overview, how it works, queries, subscribing, compute lifecycle, LISTEN/NOTIFY guide
  • Supabase: subscribing to database changes, Postgres Changes, changelog
  • Charts: rendered from the raw results with Pele

articles.title: Bun 1.4.4's bun fmt checks Prettier's own repository about 280 times faster than Prettier
articles.description: Bun 1.4.4 ships a built-in formatter. Checking Prettier's own 2,623-file source tree took 0.10-0.15s under bun fmt against 36.77s under Prettier itself, but it also silently reimplements only a short whitelist of Prettier plugins.
articles.body_html:
I pointed bun fmt --check at Prettier's own source tree expecting it to take a few seconds. It finished before I'd read the command back to myself.

Bun 1.4.4 landed on 22 October with bun fmt, a formatter built into the runtime that claims to be Prettier-compatible and to replace a handful of common Prettier plugins outright. The obvious way to test a "Prettier-compatible, much faster" claim is to point it at a real Prettier project and see whether it agrees with Prettier's own idea of correctly formatted code, and how long that agreement takes to establish.

Prettier's own repository is a good subject for this, because Prettier enforces its own style on itself: yarn lint:prettier runs prettier . --check --cache in CI, so if I check out the repository fresh, every file prettier itself tracks should already pass a Prettier check. Bun's own release post benchmarked bun fmt against exactly this repository and claimed a 2,616-file source tree took 59.7ms, against 17.1 seconds for Prettier, calling it roughly 286 times faster.

I cloned prettier/prettier at a shallow depth, pointed both tools at it with their working directory set correctly, and let them disagree with Bun's marketing copy if they wanted to.

The headline number

With --cwd pointed at the checkout, bun fmt --list-files counted 2,623 matched files, which is close enough to Bun's own 2,616 that I'm confident this is the same test they ran.

Tool Run Wall time Peak RSS
bun fmt --check 1 0.10s 48.3 MB
bun fmt --check 2 0.13s 48.5 MB
bun fmt --check 3 0.15s 48.7 MB
prettier --check 1 36.77s 519.6 MB

I only ran Prettier once. A 37-second check, repeated enough times to build a proper spread, would have eaten the time I needed for everything else, and the sandbox I was working in started refusing repeated invocations of a formatter against a cloned repository partway through this run (it treats repeatedly executing a build tool against code it didn't write as something to be cautious about, which is a reasonable thing for it to be cautious about). One run is thinner evidence than three, so take the Prettier number as a single data point rather than a settled average. It's also close enough to Bun's own claim that I don't think a second or third run would move it much: 36.77 / 0.13 is 283 times, against Bun's claimed 286.

Both tools agreed the repository needed no changes. Zero files failed either check.

What I got wrong on the way

My first attempt at this comparison crashed both tools, not just Bun's.

I ran bun fmt --check /path/to/prettier from a different working directory, passing the repository as a plain argument instead of setting --cwd. It crashed immediately:

error: Cannot load the configuration file .../tests/integration/cli/config-external-config-syntax-error/package.json:
1 | "use strict";
2 |
3 | throw new SyntaxError("THIS ERROR MESSAGE MUST COME FROM THIS syntax-error.js FILE");
              ^
SyntaxError: THIS ERROR MESSAGE MUST COME FROM THIS syntax-error.js FILE

That file exists on purpose. It's one of Prettier's own CLI tests, checking that Prettier reports a broken external config correctly, and it's listed in .prettierignore under /tests/integration/cli/. My first instinct was that I'd found a real bug in bun fmt's config resolution: it was walking into a directory the ignore file explicitly excludes.

Then I ran the exact same invocation through real Prettier, from the same wrong working directory, and it crashed too, with the same underlying error, after spending 100 seconds getting there instead of a fraction of a second. Neither tool had a bug. I had a bug: run from outside the target directory, with no --ignore-path or --cwd pointing at it, neither tool reliably finds .prettierignore next to the files it's checking, and both end up trying to load a config they were supposed to skip. Once I passed bun fmt --check --cwd <repo> and prettier <repo> --check --ignore-path <repo>/.prettierignore, both tools skipped the test fixtures correctly and the numbers above are from that corrected setup.

It isn't as Prettier-compatible as it sounds

Bun's documentation says bun fmt includes native replacements for a few well-known Prettier plugins — Tailwind class sorting, package.json key sorting, Svelte support — specifically so you don't need to install them. I wanted to know what happens with a plugin that isn't on that short list.

I wrote a .prettierrc.json referencing prettier-plugin-organize-imports, in a project where that package was never installed, alongside a file with two unused imports:

import { z } from "zod";
import   React   from "react";
const x = {a:1,   b:2};
export function hello(name:string){return `hi ${name}`}

Real Prettier refused outright:

[error] Cannot find package 'prettier-plugin-organize-imports' imported from .../noop.js

bun fmt did not refuse. It formatted the file, exit code 0, in 2.86ms, and both unused imports were gone from the output as if the plugin had actually run:

const x = { a: 1, b: 2 };
export function hello(name: string) {
  return `hi ${name}`;
}

bun fmt --doctor explains why: it lists prettier-plugin-organize-imports under "Built-in plugins". Bun recognises that specific package name and substitutes its own native reimplementation, without ever checking whether the real package is installed, or which version of it you'd have gotten.

That's a deliberate design choice and a sensible one for the handful of plugins Bun has actually reimplemented. But it means "Prettier-compatible" has a quiet asterisk: your config can name a plugin Bun has never loaded and never will, and nothing will tell you that the behaviour you're seeing is Bun's guess at what that plugin does rather than the plugin itself.

I checked where the line actually sits by using a plugin name with no native equivalent, prettier-plugin-totally-fake-xyz:

error: 1 file was not formatted because the Prettier config uses plugins that bun fmt does not include: prettier-plugin-totally-fake-xyz
  Use --allow-unsupported to format it without the plugins.

Exit code 2, nothing written. That's an honest refusal, and a better failure mode than silently guessing. The documented workaround, --allow-unsupported, did exactly what it says:

warn: prettier-plugin-totally-fake-xyz in .../.prettierrc.json has no effect because bun fmt does not include that plugin
Formatted 1 file, 0 unchanged [1.98ms]

It formatted the file, left the (genuinely fake) plugin's effect out entirely, and told me so on stderr. If your repository leans on an actual, obscure Prettier plugin that isn't Tailwind, package.json sorting or Svelte, bun fmt will tell you plainly that it can't help, rather than quietly doing the wrong thing. It's only the plugins it has decided to clone that create the risk, and that's a small, named list you can check with --doctor before you trust it on a real project.

For what it's worth, the "and more" in Bun's claim to format "JavaScript, TypeScript, CSS, HTML, JSON, YAML, Markdown and more" held up on the small CSS, Markdown and YAML files I threw at it: messy spacing, inconsistent list markers and sloppy indentation all came out correctly formatted in the same 2ms run. I didn't find anything to push back on there.

Concurrency and memory

bun fmt --check on Vite's source tree (1,589 JS/TS files, a different project that uses oxfmt rather than Prettier as its own formatter) took 0.09s wall time with 4 threads against 0.29s with --threads=1, a roughly 3.2x speedup on this machine's 4 cores. It degraded to single-threaded cleanly rather than failing, and the CPU time Bun reported (0.21-0.33s of user time against 0.10-0.15s of wall time on the Prettier repo check) confirms it's genuinely spreading work across cores rather than just being a fast single-threaded binary.

The memory gap was the largest number I measured anywhere in this test: 48MB peak for bun fmt against 519MB for Prettier, on the same 2,623-file check. Formatting is not usually a workload anyone worries about memory for, but on a CI runner with a tight memory limit, a tenfold difference like that is the kind of thing that turns a flaky job reliable.

bun fmt --check --timing on the Prettier checkout gives a phase breakdown rather than a single number, which is the closest thing to a production-facing metric this tool has:

wall: 34.4ms finding files and configs, 65.0ms formatting, 130.7ms total, 4 threads

Finding and parsing configs costs more than a quarter of the total time on a repository this size, before a single file gets formatted, which is worth knowing if you're tempted to shave milliseconds off a CI step that runs on every push.

Run it yourself 

curl -fsSL https://bun.sh/install | bash
export PATH="$HOME/.bun/bin:$PATH"

git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/prettier/prettier.git
npm install -g prettier

# Count what bun fmt will actually check
bun fmt --list-files --cwd ./prettier | wc -l

# Time each tool, pointed correctly at the checkout
time bun fmt --check --cwd ./prettier
time prettier ./prettier --check --ignore-path ./prettier/.prettierignore

# See which plugins bun fmt has reimplemented natively
bun fmt --doctor --cwd ./prettier

I ran exactly these commands, from outside the prettier directory, to get the numbers above.

What to do with this

If you're running Prettier in CI purely to check formatting, not to apply plugin-specific transforms you'd notice the absence of, bun fmt --check is very likely a safe, much faster swap, and the memory saving alone is worth it on a constrained runner.

If your .prettierrc lists any plugin at all, run bun fmt --doctor against your actual project before switching, and compare its "Built-in plugins" list against what your config names. Anything not on that list gets an honest refusal you can act on. Anything that is on the list will format successfully and silently, using Bun's own idea of what that plugin does, which may not be the one you pinned in package.json.

articles.title: Next.js Turbopack Module Federation in 2026: Sharing Code Across Micro-Frontends Without Webpack
articles.description: Module federation in Next.js now runs on Turbopack instead of webpack. Learn how to share code across micro-frontends with multi-zones, remote module consumption, and production-ready dependency strategies.
articles.body_html:
Next.js Turbopack Module Federation in 2026: Sharing Code Across Micro-Frontends Without Webpack

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

Module federation in Next.js evolved from a webpack-specific pattern into a build-system-agnostic architecture problem. Organizations that built micro-frontend systems on webpack's Module Federation plugin now face a choice: rewrite for Turbopack's bundling model or adopt Next.js multi-zones with shared dependencies. The transition exposes assumptions about runtime module sharing that developers rarely questioned until the bundler changed.

Teams discover the issue when next dev --turbo replaces their development workflow. The webpack-based Module Federation configuration stops working because Turbopack does not expose webpack's container format or runtime APIs. A micro-frontend that loaded remote modules from sibling applications now fails at build time with "Cannot find module" errors. The application compiles when switching back to webpack with next dev --webpack, but production deployments target Turbopack for its speed improvements.

The solution requires rethinking module federation as a deployment pattern rather than a bundler feature. Next.js multi-zones provide the architectural foundation: separate applications that share a domain and coordinate routing. Shared dependencies move from runtime module containers to build-time package resolution. Remote modules become deployed zones that expose routes instead of JavaScript bundles. The host application routes requests to zone applications using rewrites, and zones handle their own bundling independently.

This architectural shift delivers better isolation and simpler deployment at the cost of runtime module sharing. Each zone bundles its own dependencies, which increases total JavaScript payload when zones duplicate packages. The tradeoff favors maintainability because zones deploy independently without coordinating dependency versions at runtime.

Key Takeaways

  • Turbopack does not support webpack's Module Federation plugin or container runtime APIs.
  • Next.js multi-zones replace module federation by deploying separate applications that share a domain through routing.
  • Shared dependencies resolve at build time through monorepo package references instead of runtime module containers.
  • Each zone bundles independently, which eliminates version coordination but increases total JavaScript size.
  • Production deployments use rewrites to route paths between zones while maintaining a single user-facing domain.

Understanding Module Federation in Next.js: The Current Webpack-Based Landscape

Module federation in webpack allows separate builds to share modules at runtime. A host application loads remote modules from deployed containers without including them in its own bundle. The ModuleFederationPlugin generates container entry points that expose selected modules and define shared dependencies. When the host application imports a federated module, webpack's runtime resolves the remote container URL and loads the module dynamically.

Next.js applications use this pattern by configuring webpack in next.config.js. The configuration defines exposed modules, shared dependencies, and remote container locations. A typical setup includes a host application that consumes modules from multiple remote applications.

// next.config.js for host application with webpack module federation
const { NextFederationPlugin } = require('@module-federation/nextjs-mf');

module.exports = {
  webpack(config, options) {
    config.plugins.push(
      new NextFederationPlugin({
        name: 'host',
        remotes: {
          remote1: `remote1@${process.env.REMOTE1_URL}/_next/static/chunks/remoteEntry.js`,
          remote2: `remote2@${process.env.REMOTE2_URL}/_next/static/chunks/remoteEntry.js`,
        },
        shared: {
          react: { singleton: true, requiredVersion: '^18.0.0' },
          'react-dom': { singleton: true, requiredVersion: '^18.0.0' },
        },
      })
    );
    return config;
  },
};

The remote applications configure exposed modules that the host can import. Each remote builds a container that exports selected components and resolves shared dependencies according to the federation config.

// next.config.js for remote application
const { NextFederationPlugin } = require('@module-federation/nextjs-mf');

module.exports = {
  webpack(config, options) {
    config.plugins.push(
      new NextFederationPlugin({
        name: 'remote1',
        filename: 'static/chunks/remoteEntry.js',
        exposes: {
          './ProductCard': './components/ProductCard',
          './CheckoutButton': './components/CheckoutButton',
        },
        shared: {
          react: { singleton: true },
          'react-dom': { singleton: true },
        },
      })
    );
    return config;
  },
};

Runtime module sharing depends on webpack's container format and initialization sequence. The host application loads remote containers by injecting script tags or using dynamic imports. Webpack's runtime coordinates dependency resolution to ensure shared modules load exactly once. This works reliably when all applications use webpack with compatible container versions.

The webpack-specific implementation creates tight coupling between the bundler and the module federation architecture. Teams structure their micro-frontends around webpack's container format, which becomes a dependency that cannot be swapped without rewriting the entire system.

Module federation architecture diagram showing webpack containers

Turbopack's Architecture and What Changes for Module Federation

Turbopack replaces webpack as Next.js 16's default bundler. The architecture uses Rust-based incremental compilation with persistent caching, which delivers faster builds than webpack's JavaScript-based pipeline. Turbopack compiles only changed modules during development and caches compilation results to disk. Build times improve by 10x for large applications according to Vercel's benchmarks (Next.js 16 release notes, October 2026).

The bundler does not implement webpack's Module Federation plugin or container format. Turbopack's module system differs fundamentally from webpack's runtime architecture. Webpack generates container entry points that expose modules through a global object. Turbopack outputs ES modules with static import/export semantics that resolve at build time. There is no runtime container API to load federated modules dynamically.

Next.js 16 with Turbopack removes support for the webpack() configuration key in next.config.js. Applications that relied on webpack plugins for module federation no longer have access to the container plugin. The next dev and next build commands default to Turbopack, and the --webpack flag provides a temporary escape hatch for compatibility.

The architectural shift forces teams to reconsider how they structure micro-frontends. Runtime module federation assumed a bundler would coordinate module loading across deployed applications. Turbopack's design rejects that pattern in favor of build-time optimization and static analysis. Applications must adopt deployment-based federation where routing replaces runtime module containers.

Turbopack supports webpack loaders through a compatibility layer in the turbopack.rules configuration (Next.js Turbopack API reference, v16.1). This allows some webpack-based tooling to continue working, but does not extend to runtime plugins like Module Federation. The loader compatibility targets file transformations during compilation, not runtime module resolution.

The transition creates pressure to adopt alternative patterns that work with Turbopack's constraints. Next.js multi-zones become the primary approach for code sharing across micro-frontends. Each zone deploys as an independent application with its own Turbopack build. Zones coordinate through routing rather than module containers.

Implementing Module Federation with Next.js and Turbopack: Practical Setup

Multi-zones in Next.js provide the architectural replacement for webpack module federation. Each zone is a separate Next.js application that serves a subset of routes on a shared domain. The host application acts as the router, forwarding requests to zone applications based on URL paths. Zones deploy independently and bundle their dependencies without runtime coordination.

The setup requires configuring each zone with an assetPrefix to avoid static file conflicts. The host application defines rewrites that route paths to zone domains. A typical configuration includes three applications: a host that handles the root paths, and two zones for specialized features.

// next.config.ts for a zone application (e.g., product catalog)
import type { NextConfig } from 'next';

const config: NextConfig = {
  assetPrefix: '/catalog-static',
  async rewrites() {
    return {
      beforeFiles: [
        {
          source: '/catalog-static/_next/:path+',
          destination: '/_next/:path+',
        },
      ],
    };
  },
};

export default config;

The host application configures rewrites to forward zone paths to their deployed domains. This routes user requests to the correct application without exposing the zone URLs in the browser.

// next.config.ts for host application
import type { NextConfig } from 'next';

const config: NextConfig = {
  async rewrites() {
    return [
      {
        source: '/catalog',
        destination: `${process.env.CATALOG_ZONE_URL}/catalog`,
      },
      {
        source: '/catalog/:path+',
        destination: `${process.env.CATALOG_ZONE_URL}/catalog/:path+`,
      },
      {
        source: '/catalog-static/:path+',
        destination: `${process.env.CATALOG_ZONE_URL}/catalog-static/:path+`,
      },
      {
        source: '/checkout',
        destination: `${process.env.CHECKOUT_ZONE_URL}/checkout`,
      },
      {
        source: '/checkout/:path+',
        destination: `${process.env.CHECKOUT_ZONE_URL}/checkout/:path+`,
      },
      {
        source: '/checkout-static/:path+',
        destination: `${process.env.CHECKOUT_ZONE_URL}/checkout-static/:path+`,
      },
    ];
  },
};

export default config;

Shared code moves from runtime module federation to build-time package references. A monorepo structure with workspaces allows zones to import shared components and utilities as npm packages. Each zone includes shared packages as dependencies and Turbopack bundles them at build time.

// package.json for zone application in monorepo
{
  "name": "@company/catalog-zone",
  "dependencies": {
    "@company/ui-components": "workspace:*",
    "@company/auth-utils": "workspace:*",
    "next": "16.1.0",
    "react": "^18.3.1",
    "react-dom": "^18.3.1"
  }
}

Zones import shared components using standard ES module imports. Turbopack resolves workspace packages during compilation and includes them in each zone's bundle.

// app/catalog/page.tsx in catalog zone
import { ProductCard } from '@company/ui-components';
import { useAuth } from '@company/auth-utils';

export default function CatalogPage() {
  const { user } = useAuth();

  return (
    <div>
      <h1>Product Catalog</h1>
      {user && <p>Welcome, {user.name}</p>}
      <ProductCard
        title="Example Product"
        price={29.99}
        imageUrl="/products/example.jpg"
      />
    </div>
  );
}

This setup eliminates runtime module containers and version coordination. Each zone bundles its dependencies independently, which increases total payload size when zones duplicate packages. The tradeoff favors deployment independence and simpler dependency management.

Multi-zone architecture with shared packages

Remote Module Consumption Patterns: Host and Remote App Configuration

Remote module consumption in multi-zones requires explicit routing configuration instead of dynamic imports. The host application cannot load zone components directly because zones deploy as separate Next.js applications. Navigation between zones performs hard page loads that unload the current zone's resources and load the new zone.

Zones expose routes rather than component exports. A zone serves pages at specific paths, and the host application routes users to those paths through rewrites or standard links. The browser treats navigation to a zone as a navigation to a different part of the same domain.

// app/page.tsx in host application
import Link from 'next/link';

export default function HomePage() {
  return (
    <div>
      <h1>Welcome</h1>
      <nav>
        <Link href="/catalog">Browse Products</Link>
        <Link href="/checkout">Checkout</Link>
      </nav>
    </div>
  );
}

Clicking the link to /catalog triggers a hard navigation to the catalog zone. The host application's rewrite configuration forwards the request to the catalog zone's domain, and the browser loads the catalog zone's JavaScript bundle. This differs from webpack module federation where a federated component could render within the host's page without a navigation.

Shared data patterns require server-side coordination or external state. Zones cannot share React state or context across zone boundaries because each zone runs its own React root. Authentication tokens, user preferences, and cart data must persist in cookies, localStorage, or a backend API that all zones can access.

// lib/auth.ts shared package used by all zones
import { cookies } from 'next/headers';

export async function getUser() {
  const cookieStore = await cookies();
  const token = cookieStore.get('auth_token');

  if (!token) {
    return null;
  }

  const response = await fetch(`${process.env.API_URL}/user`, {
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token.value}` },
  });

  return response.ok ? response.json() : null;
}

Each zone calls getUser() independently to fetch user data from the backend. The function lives in a shared package that all zones import, but execution happens separately in each zone's server runtime.

Soft navigation within a zone uses Next.js's Link component normally. Navigating between pages in the same zone performs client-side routing without reloading the application. Hard navigation only occurs when crossing zone boundaries.

The pattern forces explicit boundaries between micro-frontends. Zones must define clear responsibilities and minimize cross-zone dependencies. A catalog zone handles product browsing and search. A checkout zone manages cart and payment. The host application provides navigation and shared layout elements.

Performance Comparison: Webpack Module Federation vs Turbopack-Compatible Approaches

Aspect Webpack Module Federation Turbopack Multi-Zones
Build time 60-120 seconds for host + remotes 5-15 seconds per zone (parallel builds)
Initial page load 180-250 KB (host + federation runtime) 120-180 KB per zone (no federation overhead)
Subsequent zone navigation 80-120 KB (remote container + modules) 120-180 KB (full page with new bundle)
Shared dependency handling Runtime version negotiation Build-time resolution (duplicated across zones)
Hot module reload 2-5 seconds (webpack HMR) 50-500 milliseconds (Turbopack incremental)
Deploy coordination Must align dependency versions across remotes Independent zone deploys

Webpack module federation delivers smaller initial payloads when multiple remotes share dependencies. The federation runtime loads React once and reuses it across all federated components. Each remote module adds only its unique code to the total JavaScript size. This optimization matters when a host application loads five or more remote modules from different teams.

Turbopack multi-zones duplicate shared dependencies across zone bundles. If three zones each use React, React ships three times. The duplication increases total JavaScript by 40-60 KB per additional zone for typical React applications. The cost compounds with additional shared dependencies like state management libraries or UI frameworks.

Build performance favors Turbopack by a significant margin. Each zone builds independently in parallel, and Turbopack's incremental compilation completes in seconds. Webpack module federation requires coordinating builds across all federated applications and waiting for the slowest remote to finish. Large organizations with 10-15 micro-frontends see build pipelines complete 5-10x faster with multi-zones.

Development experience improves with Turbopack's hot module reload speed. Changes to zone code reflect in the browser within 500 milliseconds. Webpack HMR takes 2-5 seconds for equivalent updates in federated applications. The difference compounds during feature development where developers make hundreds of small changes per day.

The navigation model trades client-side routing for simpler architecture. Webpack module federation loads remote modules without page navigation, which feels faster to users moving between micro-frontends. Multi-zones perform hard navigations that reload the entire page. The perceived slowdown disappears for applications where zones represent distinct user workflows with infrequent transitions.

Version coordination becomes simpler with multi-zones. Each zone deploys independently with its own dependency versions. Breaking changes in shared packages affect only the zones that have not upgraded. Webpack module federation requires all remotes to coordinate React and shared library versions to avoid runtime conflicts. The coordination overhead grows with team count.

Production Patterns: Shared Dependencies, Versioning, and Error Boundaries

Shared dependencies in multi-zones require build-time coordination through package versioning. Monorepo workspaces allow zones to depend on shared packages that reference the same version. Breaking changes in shared code require updating all consuming zones before deployment.

// packages/ui-components/package.json
{
  "name": "@company/ui-components",
  "version": "3.2.0",
  "peerDependencies": {
    "react": "^18.3.0",
    "react-dom": "^18.3.0"
  }
}

Zones specify workspace dependencies using the workspace:* protocol. This ensures all zones use the same version of shared packages without duplicating package code in the repository.

// apps/catalog-zone/package.json
{
  "dependencies": {
    "@company/ui-components": "workspace:*",
    "@company/analytics": "workspace:*"
  }
}

Version conflicts surface at build time rather than runtime. If a zone attempts to import an incompatible shared package version, the build fails with a clear error message. This prevents the subtle runtime failures that occur with webpack module federation when remotes load conflicting dependency versions.

Error boundaries protect against zone failures at the routing level. If a zone crashes or fails to load, the host application can display a fallback UI instead of a broken page. This requires implementing error handling in the zone's root layout.

// app/layout.tsx in zone application
import { ErrorBoundary } from '@company/ui-components';

export default function ZoneLayout({
  children,
}: {
  children: React.ReactNode;
}) {
  return (
    <ErrorBoundary
      fallback={
        <div>
          <h1>Something went wrong</h1>
          <p>We are working to fix this issue.</p>
          <a href="/">Return to home</a>
        </div>
      }
    >
      {children}
    </ErrorBoundary>
  );
}

The error boundary catches React errors within the zone and renders the fallback UI. This prevents a crashed zone from breaking the entire application. Users can navigate back to the host or other zones even when one zone fails.

Network errors during zone navigation require server-side fallbacks. If a zone's server becomes unavailable, the host application's rewrite returns a 502 error. Next.js middleware can intercept these errors and redirect to a maintenance page.

// middleware.ts in host application
import { NextResponse } from 'next/server';
import type { NextRequest } from 'next/server';

export async function middleware(request: NextRequest) {
  const zonePaths = ['/catalog', '/checkout'];
  const isZonePath = zonePaths.some(path => 
    request.nextUrl.pathname.startsWith(path)
  );

  if (isZonePath) {
    try {
      const response = await fetch(request.url, {
        method: request.method,
        headers: request.headers,
      });

      if (!response.ok) {
        return NextResponse.redirect(new URL('/maintenance', request.url));
      }

      return response;
    } catch (error) {
      return NextResponse.redirect(new URL('/maintenance', request.url));
    }
  }

  return NextResponse.next();
}

Observability for multi-zones requires tracing requests across zone boundaries. Each zone should emit structured logs that include a request ID propagated through rewrites. The host application generates the request ID and passes it to zones via headers.

// middleware.ts in host application
import { NextResponse } from 'next/server';
import type { NextRequest } from 'next/server';
import { randomUUID } from 'crypto';

export function middleware(request: NextRequest) {
  const requestId = randomUUID();
  const requestHeaders = new Headers(request.headers);
  requestHeaders.set('x-request-id', requestId);

  return NextResponse.next({
    request: { headers: requestHeaders },
  });
}

Zones extract the request ID from headers and include it in log output. This allows correlating errors across zone boundaries when debugging production issues.

Dependency optimization reduces bundle duplication when multiple zones share heavy libraries. The optimizePackageImports option in next.config.ts tells Turbopack to tree-shake package imports, which eliminates unused code from bundles (Next.js package bundling guide, v16.1).

// next.config.ts for zone application
import type { NextConfig } from 'next';

const config: NextConfig = {
  experimental: {
    optimizePackageImports: ['@mui/material', 'lodash', 'date-fns'],
  },
};

export default config;

This configuration reduces bundle size by 20-40 KB for zones that import only a subset of package exports. The optimization applies per zone, which means each zone still bundles its own copy of shared packages but with only the required code.

Server actions require explicit origin allowlists when zones share a domain. Next.js validates the origin header for server action requests to prevent CSRF attacks. The host domain must appear in each zone's allowedOrigins configuration (Next.js server actions configuration, v16.0).

// next.config.ts for zone application
import type { NextConfig } from 'next';

const config: NextConfig = {
  experimental: {
    serverActions: {
      allowedOrigins: ['example.com', 'www.example.com'],
    },
  },
};

export default config;

Without this configuration, server actions in zones fail with CSRF errors when the zone serves requests proxied through the host domain.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can Turbopack load webpack module federation containers?

No. Turbopack does not implement webpack's container format or runtime APIs. Applications using webpack module federation must either continue using webpack with the --webpack flag or migrate to multi-zones.

How do multi-zones handle shared React state?

Zones cannot share React state directly because each zone runs its own React root. Shared state requires external storage like cookies, localStorage, or a backend API that all zones access.

Do multi-zones work with third-party deployed micro-frontends?

Yes. Zones can route to any deployed application using rewrites. The remote application does not need to be a Next.js zone as long as it serves content at the routed path.

What happens when a zone deployment fails?

Failed zone deployments do not affect other zones. The host application continues serving its routes and other zones. Users navigating to the failed zone see errors only when accessing that zone's paths.

Can zones share Next.js middleware?

No. Each zone executes its own middleware independently. Shared middleware logic must be extracted to a package that zones import and execute separately.

Conclusion: The Future of Micro-Frontends in Next.js

Multi-zones replace runtime module federation with deployment-based architecture. The pattern aligns with Turbopack's build-time optimization model and removes the complexity of runtime module coordination. Organizations gain faster builds, independent zone deployments, and simpler dependency management at the cost of larger total JavaScript payloads.

The architectural shift requires rethinking micro-frontend boundaries. Zones work best when they represent distinct user workflows with infrequent navigation between them. Applications that require frequent component-level code sharing across teams may find the hard navigation overhead expensive. Those cases benefit from extracting shared code to packages rather than attempting runtime module sharing.

Turbopack's adoption as Next.js's default bundler makes multi-zones the standard approach for micro-frontends in the Next.js ecosystem. The webpack-based module federation pattern remains available through the --webpack flag but receives no optimization attention from the framework. Teams building new micro-frontend architectures should design around multi-zones from the start.

For further exploration of Next.js architectural patterns, see related posts on Next.js 15 caching changes, Next.js 16 form component progressive enhancement, and Next.js 16 instrumentation stable.

articles.title: Delete Confirmation Dialogs: Show the Exit Path in Your Public SaaS Demo
articles.description: A useful public demo of a delete confirmation dialog should show which item will be affected, what...
articles.body_html:
A useful public demo of a delete confirmation dialog should show which item will be affected, what deletion means, and how someone leaves without deleting anything. Record the safe exit as well as the final action. A screenshot of a red button cannot show whether backing out preserves the work or whether the interface tells the truth about recovery.

For a developer building a SaaS in public, this gives founder peers a concrete interaction to review. It also exposes questions that belong in implementation checks rather than a discussion about button color. Use prepared data and a suitable test environment for the demonstration.

The project-deletion flow below is fictional. It is a review method, not a report of testing an actual product. No action in a demo should affect real customer work, and a simulated result should be labelled as simulated.

Define exactly what the delete action affects

Imagine a small planning app with projects and tasks. Its current design allows the owner to delete a project. Before asking anyone to review the dialog, the developer needs to know whether this also removes tasks, attachments, shared access, or references elsewhere in the app.

Write that behavior in ordinary language. If the implementation archives a project and permits restoration, describe that behavior. If it permanently removes the project, do not borrow reassuring language from an archive flow.

The interface and the underlying behavior must agree. A dialog that says “Remove from this view” creates a different expectation from one that says “Delete this project and its tasks.” Changing the label alone cannot resolve an uncertain backend operation.

Keep the review scoped to one action. Deleting a task, leaving a shared project, and deleting a whole workspace can have different consequences. A public demo becomes hard to assess when it switches between those operations without explaining the difference.

Start the recording before the dialog opens

Show the project in its normal context and the control that opens the confirmation. A viewer should be able to tell which project the action concerns before reading the dialog.

In the fictional app, use a prepared project with a neutral name and sample tasks. Say that the data is prepared for the demo. Don't include real project names or customer material merely to make the recording look realistic.

Open the dialog and pause long enough for someone to read it. Avoid editing out the transition if that hides where focus goes or makes it unclear whether the dialog has already performed the action.

Ask a reviewer what they think has happened so far. They may interpret opening the dialog as the deletion itself, especially if the background item disappears early. That is a specific point to investigate rather than a general verdict on whether the design looks modern.

Make the target and consequence visible together

A generic “Are you sure?” prompt asks the person to remember the action and its scope. In the example, the dialog can name the prepared project and explain the actual consequence beside the final button.

Use only information the application can support. If the dialog displays a task count, check that the count refers to the affected tasks under the current conditions. A convincing number that is stale or calculated from another scope can make the prompt less trustworthy.

Don't add a list of alarming consequences simply to make the interaction feel serious. Name the consequences that actually apply. The point is to help someone decide, not to create a dramatic warning around every small action.

A peer review question can be direct: “Which item do you think will be removed, and what else do you expect to happen?” The answer reveals the viewer's interpretation before you explain the intended one.

Record the path that keeps the project intact

First demonstrate backing out. Use the non-destructive control, then show the original project and its tasks still present. If the interface offers more than one way to dismiss the dialog, inspect those paths separately.

The label for leaving should fit the operation. A dialog about cancelling a scheduled job can make “Cancel” ambiguous. In your own flow, check whether a reader can distinguish cancelling the dialog from performing the action described in it.

A visible return to the project is stronger evidence for this one path than simply closing the modal. It still does not prove that every dismissal path is safe. Keyboard input, clicking outside, navigation, or a connection problem may exercise different behavior.

Keep those unresolved paths in the review notes. Public feedback can help identify the questions; implementation checks establish what the actual system does. Do not describe an untested path as safe because the main recording ended well.

Review keyboard and assistive-technology behavior separately

The W3C alert-dialog pattern describes an interrupting modal message that obtains a response. It explains the role, label and description relationships, and warns that marking a dialog modal must match how it actually behaves.

This guidance is useful when reviewing a confirmation, but a video of the screen cannot establish that its semantics work. Inspect the dialog's accessible name and description, focus behavior, available controls, and the return from dismissal in the actual implementation.

Use the appropriate dialog pattern for the interaction rather than adding an alert role for emphasis. A semantic label is not decoration. It communicates behavior to software and people using assistive technology.

Report the checks you performed and the ones you did not. A short public clip may show a keyboard path while leaving screen-reader behavior for a separate check. That is a useful bounded artifact without claiming that the whole application meets an accessibility standard.

Show completion without implying an undo that does not exist

Only after reviewing the safe exit should the prepared demo show the final deletion path. Reopen the dialog for the same prepared project, confirm the action, and show the resulting state.

If the system supports restoration, demonstrate the actual supported restoration route in another bounded sequence. If it does not, say that clearly. Do not put an “Undo” control into a mockup and present it as proof that recovery works.

Check what a person sees if completion is uncertain. A slow response, repeated click, or stale list can leave the interface out of step with the operation. Those questions may need a separate test rather than a longer public recording of the happy path.

The completion message should describe the operation you can verify. A disappearing card alone does not tell you whether related data was removed, access changed, or the backend accepted the action exactly once.

Ask peers one question about the decision

Share the demo with a specific uncertainty: the target, the scope, the non-destructive exit, or the meaning of the result. Asking “Any thoughts?” invites people to review a different problem from the one you need to resolve.

Buildside is the community context here. Uriel Bitton builds and runs Buildside, which is this article's publisher relationship. Wherever you request feedback, give peers enough task context to judge the interaction without assuming they know the implementation.

A peer may understand the dialog perfectly and still lack the customer's workflow. Another may point out a risk you had not considered. Treat each response as a scoped observation or suggestion, then decide which question needs further evidence.

Don't turn agreement about the wording into proof that accidental deletion will never occur. Clear communication and reliable behavior are both part of the interaction, and each needs appropriate checks.

Keep a review record that survives the next redesign

Save the version reviewed, the prepared data conditions, the question asked, and what changed. Attach the relevant recording or screenshots to your own development notes so a later visual redesign does not lose the reasoning.

For the fictional project flow, the record might say that the dialog now names the project and that the recorded safe exit returns to the intact task list. It should separately list any unresolved recovery or keyboard question.

A follow-up build-in-public update can show the specific revision and the behavior verified. Avoid claiming a drop in user mistakes unless you have measured that outcome under a suitable method.

The useful public artifact shows a real choice with an understandable consequence and exit. That gives other founders a precise way to help and gives the developer a concrete interaction to revisit as the product changes.

Hey I'm Uriel Bitton. I write about building in public strategies and growing startups.

Subscribe for more stories on growing your audience by building in public.

Join us on Buildside: the social network for founders building in public.
