articles.body_html:
Imagine spending your weekend building something interesting.

Maybe a small weather application.

A tool that organizes your photographs.

A website that recreates the interface of an old computer.

Or a simple Python script that solves a problem nobody else seems to care about.

You spend hours experimenting.

Something breaks.

You fix it.

You learn something new.

And finally, the project works.

You're happy.

Then someone asks:

"That's interesting. How are you planning to monetize it?"

And suddenly, a perfectly enjoyable weekend project becomes a business discussion.

What's the target market?

What's the revenue model?

How will you acquire users?

Can you scale it?

Is there an investor opportunity?

I understand these questions. I'm a founder myself.

But I've been thinking about something lately.

Why does everything we build need to become something we sell?

We Have Turned Building Into a Business Competition

There was a time when building software was also a way to explore technology.

You learned HTML because you wanted to create a website.

You experimented with Python because you were curious about automation.

You built a game because you enjoyed playing games.

You created a small tool because something bothered you and you wanted to fix it.

Not every project needed customers.

Not every experiment needed a market.

Not every repository needed thousands of stars.

Sometimes, the project existed for one reason.

You wanted to see whether you could build it.

But the conversation around software development has changed.

Today, we frequently hear:

Build in public.

Launch an MVP.

Find paying users.

Create recurring revenue.

Turn your skills into a business.

There's nothing wrong with any of these ideas.

In fact, I believe they're valuable when you're intentionally building a company.

The problem begins when we start applying the same expectations to every experiment.

A Side Project Has a Different Job

A startup exists to create value for customers through a sustainable business.

A side project doesn't necessarily have that responsibility.

It might exist to help you learn.

To explore an unfamiliar technology.

To understand how something works.

To test an unusual idea.

Or simply to enjoy the process of creating something.

Consider someone building a tiny operating system as a learning exercise.

It probably won't compete with Linux or Windows.

Does that mean the project has failed?

Of course not.

The developer might learn more about memory management, process scheduling, and hardware than they would from months of watching tutorials.

Or consider someone building a small application that visualizes sorting algorithms.

There are already hundreds of similar tools.

From a business perspective, the idea might appear unoriginal.

From a learning perspective, it could be incredibly valuable.

A project's value isn't always measured by how many people will pay for it.

Sometimes its value is what it teaches the person building it.

AI Has Made This Pressure Even More Interesting

AI has reduced many of the barriers to creating software.

You can prototype an idea faster.

Generate boilerplate.

Explore unfamiliar frameworks.

Build interfaces.

Experiment with APIs.

That's wonderful.

But there's a strange consequence.

Because building has become easier, the pressure to produce something commercially useful can become even greater.

Why build a small experiment when you could launch an application?

Why learn a framework when you could create a SaaS product?

Why spend time exploring an idea when you could turn it into a business?

I think this misses something important.

Just because technology makes an opportunity possible doesn't mean we have to pursue it.

We should be able to experiment without having to justify every hour through a potential financial return.

Otherwise, curiosity slowly turns into another performance target.

Sometimes the Most Interesting Projects Are Completely Impractical

Think about the projects developers enjoy sharing.

Someone creates a programming language for fun.

Someone builds a robot that performs a ridiculous task.

Someone turns a terminal into a game.

Someone recreates an old interface.

Someone connects a sensor to a Raspberry Pi just to understand how it works.

These projects may not solve enormous business problems.

But they can be fascinating.

They encourage experimentation.

They teach unexpected lessons.

And sometimes they inspire other developers to try something new.

Not everything useful has to begin with a commercial purpose.

In fact, some of the most interesting ideas emerge when people are free to experiment without knowing exactly where the results will lead.

That's one reason I don't want us to lose the culture of building things simply because they seem interesting.

I Believe in Distribution. But Not Everything Needs Distribution.

This is where my perspective as a founder becomes important.

I've written before about how developers can build global influence without working at Big Tech.

I believe in sharing knowledge.

I believe in building relationships.

I believe developers should understand how to reach people with their work.

And when you're building a company, distribution is absolutely essential.

A product that nobody discovers will struggle, regardless of its technical quality.

But here's an important distinction.

A project you build for learning is not the same as a product you're building for customers.

The first doesn't need a marketing strategy.

The second probably does.

The first can succeed even if only one person uses it.

The second needs a sustainable reason to exist in the market.

Both are legitimate.

The mistake is pretending they're the same thing.

The Hidden Cost of Monetizing Every Idea

Turning an experiment into a business changes your responsibilities.

Suppose you build a small application over the weekend.

You enjoy the process.

You share it with a few friends.

Everything is simple.

Now imagine deciding to commercialize it.

Suddenly, you may need:

  • customer support and documentation
  • billing and payment systems
  • security and privacy considerations
  • reliable hosting and monitoring
  • maintenance and updates
  • marketing and customer acquisition
  • financial and operational planning

None of these responsibilities are inherently bad.

They're part of building a real product.

But they can fundamentally change your relationship with the project.

Something that previously gave you creative freedom can become another obligation.

And sometimes, the financial opportunity isn't large enough to justify everything that comes with it.

A side project can be successful precisely because it remains a side project.

We Shouldn't Confuse Learning With Wasted Time

Imagine a developer spending two weeks creating a small game.

They don't sell it.

They don't launch a startup.

They don't gain a large audience.

But they learn about state management, event handling, rendering, and application architecture.

Was that time wasted?

I don't think so.

The project might make them a better developer.

It might introduce them to a new field.

It might help them discover something they genuinely enjoy.

And that learning could become valuable years later in a completely different context.

Not every return on effort is immediate.

Not every useful skill can be assigned a price.

Sometimes the most valuable outcome is that you understand something today that you didn't understand yesterday.

There's Nothing Wrong With Wanting to Build a Business

I don't want this article to sound anti-startup.

Quite the opposite.

Building a business is one of the most challenging and rewarding things someone can attempt.

I know that entrepreneurship requires discipline, patience, judgment, and an enormous amount of work that happens outside the technical product.

If your intention is to create a business, you should think about customers, distribution, pricing, competition, and financial sustainability.

You should validate demand.

You should understand the market.

You should ask whether the problem is valuable enough for someone to pay to solve it.

But you don't need to apply that process to every interesting idea.

I wrote in I Think Developers Are Building Too Much Software about the importance of knowing what deserves to be built.

There's another side to that argument.

Sometimes something deserves to be built even when it has no commercial value.

Because the purpose might be learning, creativity, or enjoyment.

And those are perfectly valid reasons.

Maybe We Need Two Different Definitions of Success

For commercial products, success might mean:

Are customers using it?

Does it solve a valuable problem?

Will people pay for it?

Can the business sustain itself?

For personal projects, the questions can be different.

Did I learn something?

Did I solve an interesting challenge?

Did I enjoy building it?

Would I like to explore this technology further?

Did it make me a better thinker or developer?

We need both kinds of work in the technology community.

Commercial projects create economic opportunities.

Personal experiments create space for curiosity and discovery.

And occasionally, something built purely out of curiosity becomes a useful product.

That's wonderful when it happens.

But it doesn't need to be the expectation.

My Advice to Developers: Keep Something Just for Yourself

If you're a developer, I would encourage you to have at least one project that doesn't need to prove anything to anyone.

No business model.

No growth target.

No investor pitch.

No pressure to make it viral.

Build something because you find it fascinating.

Experiment with a language you've never used.

Recreate something from your childhood.

Build a useless little tool that makes you smile.

Explore a difficult algorithm.

Try combining two technologies that don't normally belong together.

You might discover something useful.

You might build something terrible.

You might abandon the project halfway through.

That's fine.

Not every experiment needs to become a success story.

Sometimes the freedom to fail without financial consequences is exactly what makes experimentation worthwhile.

The Best Part of Building Might Be the Building Itself

I spend a lot of time thinking about technology, business, and the future of AI.

I believe technology should solve meaningful problems.

I believe founders should think seriously about distribution and customer value.

And I believe developers should recognize the opportunities their skills create.

But I also believe we need to preserve something simple.

The joy of creating things.

Not because someone will pay us.

Not because it will improve our personal brand.

Not because an algorithm will reward us.

But because solving a problem, understanding a system, or making an idea come alive can be satisfying in its own right.

We don't have to turn every interest into income.

We don't have to turn every experiment into a product.

And we certainly don't have to turn every side project into a startup.

Sometimes you can build something, learn something, smile at what you've created, and move on.

That's not a missed business opportunity. That's a perfectly good reason to build.

articles.title: I Had No Idea What Was Eating My Mac’s Storage, So I Built Something to Show Me
articles.description: My Mac said 179.58 GB of 245.11 GB used. Applications made sense. Documents made sense. But a huge...
articles.body_html:
My Mac said 179.58 GB of 245.11 GB used. Applications made sense. Documents made sense. But a huge gray block labeled System Data took up more space than everything else combined, and macOS wouldn't tell me what was inside it.

I got tired of guessing, so I decided to build something that would show me everything and let me act on it. The next few days looked a lot like this:

How it came together

The first version was a plain CLI, built with a bit of help from my friend, AI.

It worked, but only just. It listed files under 10 MB, had no color, and nothing was organized.

So I went back and looked for libraries that could present the output properly, and rich was a big help. The second version was decent, but it still felt like something was missing.

Next I wondered whether the output could be interactive. It turned out I could connect a web interface to the Python side and route everything through it. That was a real improvement, but still not quite there.

A bit more digging showed me I could wrap that web interface in a native window. That's how it became a proper macOS app, which I built for myself first.

Then I opened Mac Deep Cleaner, the tool I'd made for exactly this problem, and let it scan my own machine.

It found a lot. More importantly, it showed me where every gigabyte lived, so I didn't have to guess. That's the whole idea: a cleaner that opens the box and lets you decide, instead of deleting things you never got to see.

The one rule

Never delete anything the user hasn't reviewed.

Everything else grew out of that sentence:

  • Files go to Finder's Trash, not straight into oblivion.
  • Before anything moves, every cleanup is checked against scan generation tokens, exact file IDs, inode matches, and path restrictions.
  • System files (com.apple.*, SIP-protected paths, running app bundles) are locked and can't be touched.
  • There's no cloud analytics. Everything runs on your machine.

What the scan found on my Mac

When you launch it, you get a local dashboard that tells you the truth right away.

Across 68 items, it found 34.63 GB that could be reclaimed. The split underneath that headline number matters more:

  • Safe to remove: 41.39 MB
  • Review first: 32.90 GB
  • Needs care: 1.69 GB

I could have made that headline far more exciting by auto-selecting everything. Instead, only the tiny safe slice is one click away. The big chunk is marked "Review first" because the tool can't know what matters to you, and I think that honesty is the whole point of the product.

Seeing inside your apps

The part I'm proudest of is the Application Analyzer. Pick any app and it shows the full footprint, not just the .app bundle.

Take VS Code, which uses 3.01 GB in total. The app bundle is 1.5 GB and Application Support is another 1.51 GB. The caches, the part that's truly regenerable, are only 2.28 MB. A lot of people assume clearing caches frees up gigabytes, and here you can see it doesn't. You get to decide with real numbers.

It also notices when an app is running and tells you to quit it before uninstalling. It's a small detail, but it saves you from a bad afternoon.

Under the hood

For the curious:

  • The core is Python 3.9+, installable with pip install mac-deep-cleaner.
  • A local web dashboard is served on a loopback port.
  • A Swift window shell provides native macOS chrome and full-screen support.
  • Scanning is multi-threaded, with content hashing for duplicate detection.
  • One tool, three commands: mac-deep-cleaner, mac-cleaner, and mdc.

What's new in v3.0.5

This release is all about polish, the things you only notice when they're wrong:

  • I fixed the missing top inset in browser mode, without disturbing native window and full-screen spacing.
  • The dashboard, favicon, README, and macOS icon now all use a single assets/app_icon.png, and I removed the redundant branding images.
  • Shared assets now ship in Python distributions and standalone macOS builds.
  • The CLI and native bundle versions come from one package version constant, so they can't drift apart.

Installing it

Option 1: Download the app (easiest)

Grab Mac-Deep-Cleaner-macOS.zip (about 9.7 MB) from the v3.0.5 release page.

Unzip it and drag Mac Deep Cleaner.app into your /Applications folder. Each release asset shows a SHA-256 checksum, so you can verify your download:

shasum -a 256 ~/Downloads/Mac-Deep-Cleaner-macOS.zip

The output should match the checksum on the release page.

Option 2: Install with pip 

pip install mac-deep-cleaner
mdc

Option 3: Build from source 

git clone https://github.com/NK2552003/Mac-Cleaner.git
cd Mac-Cleaner
python3 scripts/build_mac.py

About the macOS warning

The downloadable app isn't notarized by Apple yet, so macOS may tell you it's "damaged" or can't be opened. It isn't damaged. Gatekeeper is just being cautious about a downloaded app that hasn't been notarized.

If you got it from the official release page, move it to /Applications and run:

xattr -d com.apple.quarantine "/Applications/Mac Deep Cleaner.app"

This only removes the download-quarantine flag from that one app. If you'd rather skip Terminal, right-click the app, choose Open, and confirm. Please only do this with builds from the official repo. Notarization is on my to-do list. (The pip install doesn't have this problem.)

What I learned

  1. Trust is a feature. Showing "Review first: 32.90 GB" instead of a giant green button made the tool feel more useful, not less.
  2. Boring consistency matters. One icon file, one version constant. Half of v3.0.5 was just deleting duplication.
  3. Local-first is a relief. No servers, no accounts, and nothing leaves your machine.

Try it, break it, tell me

It's open source under Apache 2.0:

  • Download: https://github.com/NK2552003/Mac-Cleaner/releases/tag/v3.0.5
  • GitHub: https://github.com/NK2552003/Mac-Cleaner
  • PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/mac-deep-cleaner/

If you find an app footprint it misses, or a path it should protect, open an issue. And if it frees up some space for you, a star helps more than you'd think.

So, what's the most surprising thing taking up space on your Mac?

Happing Coding ;)

articles.title: Is Rec Room Shutting Down? The Real Reason a $3.5B Platform Collapsed
articles.description: TL;DR    Rec Room is not "shutting down" anymore. It already did, at noon Pacific on June 1,...
articles.body_html:
TL;DR

  • Rec Room is not "shutting down" anymore. It already did, at noon Pacific on June 1, 2026.
  • There was no single cause. The company said its costs "always ended up overwhelming the revenue we brought in."
  • It had 150 million+ players over a decade and a $3.5 billion valuation in 2021, but never became sustainably profitable.
  • Snap acquired "select assets" and some staff. The platform itself was not revived.
  • For developers, the lessons are about unit economics, moderation costs, and giving users an exit.

If you searched "is Rec Room shutting down?" this year, the answer changed from "maybe" to "yes" to "done" in about two months. The company announced the closure on March 30, 2026, and the servers went dark on June 1.

That is a strange ending for a platform that reached more than 150 million players and was valued at $3.5 billion in its December 2021 Series F. This article pulls together what the company and the press have actually said, separates confirmed facts from speculation, and draws out what developers building user-generated content (UGC) platforms can take from it. Everything here is current as of October 30, 2026.

What happened, in order

The collapse took about 15 months from the first layoff to the final shutdown.

Date What happened
Jun 1, 2026 Servers go offline at noon Pacific. The rec.net site closes, and an end-credits video is published.
May 18, 2026 Creators stop earning tokens; a final creator payout follows on June 1.
May 1, 2026 Token purchases end, and Partnered Creator registrations stop. Refund requests open (May 1 to June 15).
Mar 30, 2026 Rec Room announces the shutdown. Snap confirms it acquired "select assets" and that some staff will join its Specs Inc. hardware subsidiary.
Aug 25, 2025 About half of the staff are cut (141 positions), leaving just over 100 employees.
Mar 2025 First layoff round, affecting 16% of staff.
Dec 2021 Series F at a $3.5 billion valuation. The company raised $294 million across six rounds in total.

Sources: the company's shutdown post, GeekWire's shutdown report, GeekWire on the Snap deal and Road to VR on the 2025 layoffs.

The real reason: there wasn't just one

Headlines love a single villain, but the public record points to several problems stacking up. The company's own summary was blunt: it "never quite figured out how to make Rec Room a sustainably profitable business," and it blamed "the recent shift in the VR market, along with broader headwinds in gaming."

Here is what the reporting adds.

Popularity did not equal revenue.

The 150 million figure counts players over a decade, not people logging in today. The company said millions still played monthly, far fewer than the headline number. A free-to-play social hub still pays for servers, moderation and live operations for every active user.

The platform tried to be everything.

In its August 2025 layoff post, the company said its goal of a creation platform across VR, PC, consoles and mobile proved too ambitious. Mobile and console users produced millions of creations, but they were generally low-quality and poorly optimized, which strained the team. Co-founder Cameron Brown said the company was "narrowing our focus away from 'everyone can create' in favor of serving our very best creators," and described the company as too small for the universal vision but too big to pivot quickly.

Creator revenue grew, but not enough.

According to GeekWire, UGC revenue grew about 70% year over year as of September 2025, and creators earned more than $1 million in a single quarter for the first time. But Rec Room kept about 30 cents of each UGC dollar versus 70 cents on first-party content, so the fastest-growing line was also the thinnest.

AI features may have cost more than they earned.

GeekWire's report says per-user AI costs exceeded subscription revenue. That claim is the reporter's own narration with no date or named source, so treat it as a signal rather than a number.

What we still don't know.

Rec Room never published detailed financials. Nobody outside the company can say how close it came to a different outcome, so be wary of any post, including this one, that claims to know the one true cause.

What it meant for creators, players and staff

A shutdown tests a platform's promises. Here is how Rec Room handled the exit, based on its own announcement.

Creators lost new monetization immediately after the March announcement and stopped earning tokens on May 18. A final creator payout was processed on June 1. Working copies of rooms could not be downloaded once the servers went offline, so creators had to export room and invention data through the Steam PC build before June 1. After the announcement, a small internal team also built tools to export rooms and avatars in standard file formats, GeekWire reported. Road to VR noted that creators could use the exports to recreate rooms in Unity.

Players could no longer spend tokens after June 1. Gift cards were redeemable until April 30, refund requests for unused wallet funds ran from May 1 to June 15, and subscribers on three-, six-, and 12-month Rec Room Plus plans were refunded for unused time. Monthly subscribers had to cancel recurring payments themselves.

The community did not wait for an official successor. GeekWire reports that players uploaded their in-game report cards to fan sites to sign like yearbooks, and that unofficial fan-run servers are trying to keep versions of the game playable. No official successor was announced, and VRChat's co-founders said it "is not going anywhere."

Staff was split. Some joined Snap's Specs Inc. unit, while others are listed on a "Rec Room Grads" site seeking new roles. Snap has not disclosed how many people it hired, what it paid, or exactly which assets it bought.

Seven lessons for developers

These are my takeaways from the public record, not claims Rec Room made about itself.

  1. Track active users, not lifetime users: 150 million lifetime players and "millions" of monthly players are very different businesses. Put active users and cost per active user on your main dashboard.
  2. Count moderation as a core cost: UGC platforms pay for every creation someone uploads, whether anyone plays it or not. Rec Room said reviewing low-quality content strained its team.
  3. Know your take rate before you scale it: If the fastest-growing revenue line keeps 30 cents on the dollar and your biggest cost line grows with users, growth alone will not close the gap.
  4. Treat AI features as cost of goods sold: If inference cost per user can exceed what a subscription brings in, as GeekWire reports for Rec Room, price the feature or cap its usage before launch.
  5. Narrow the platform early: Supporting VR, PC, console, and mobile multiplied the surface area for bugs, content, and support. Each platform needs its own quality bar.
  6. Build the exit path before you need it: Rec Room built export tools after it announced the closure, with a hard deadline attached. If you run a platform, ship open-format export while you still have a full team.
  7. If you build on someone else's platform, keep your source outside it: Creators who held assets in standard formats could move on more easily. Everyone else depended on an export window that closed on June 1.

None of this means UGC platforms cannot work. It means the numbers have to work at the scale you are actually at, not the scale on your pitch deck.

The bottom line

Rec Room is gone, and the cause was ordinary rather than mysterious: a large audience, a cost base that grew with it, and revenue lines that never caught up. The company says it "spent a long time trying to find a way to make the numbers work." For the people who built rooms there, the loss is real even without a villain.

Your turn: have you built on a UGC platform that shut down or changed its rules? What would you have wanted exported, and when? Tell us in the comments.

Sources

  • School's Out for Rec Room (official announcement)
  • GeekWire: Rec Room shutting down, once valued at $3.5B
  • GeekWire: Snap acquires assets from Rec Room
  • GeekWire: Rec Room's final day
  • GeekWire: Rec Room lays off half its staff
  • Road to VR: layoffs and low-quality content (Aug 2025)
  • Road to VR: shutdown and Snap report
  • Fast Company: shutting down despite 150 million users
  • Final Boss: 150M players, still shutting down

articles.title: The Soak That Reported 5,003 Deliveries for 5,000 Records
articles.description: 5,003 deliveries. 5,000 records. Three extra.  In a streaming system whose entire pitch is the store...
articles.body_html:
5,003 deliveries. 5,000 records. Three extra.

In a streaming system whose entire pitch is the store is the truth, that's the scariest output a test can produce. Three duplicate deliveries means somewhere, something sent twice. It means exactly-once is once-short. My first annotation in the field test log was: real defect — duplicate deliveries.

The root cause turned out to be three records I put there myself. And the part I want to keep from this isn't the bug — it's that the gate flagged a genuine inconsistency, and the inconsistency was in my test's fence, not the product's.

This is from the agentwatch v0.2.1 release — the agent-security tool in agentic-suite. Full forensics in the v0.2.0 field test report.

What the soak does

The case is FT-STR-2, the drop-consumer reconciliation. The scenario it models is the one that actually keeps streaming systems honest: the consumer — the thing watching the record stream — dies mid-stream. Crashes, loses its place, comes back. What did it miss?

The test streams 5,000 events through the live tail, kills the consumer partway, lets the store keep ingesting, restarts, and then reconciles: what the consumer was told it received versus what the store actually holds. If those diverge, the operator's view is lying about the record. That's the whole trust proposition.

The original assertion on this case was comfortable:

delivered >= records   # "no store loss" — the consumer saw everything

Fine as far as it goes. Also — as the hardening pass immediately demonstrated — not the actual contract.

The stricter gate was already in the product

The product has its own reconciliation predicate, within_bounds. Not delivered >= records. delivered == records. Exactly. Because for this store, "I delivered more than I hold records for" isn't a success condition — it's an accounting error. Deliveries that exceed records mean something is being counted that was never recorded, which is a different way of saying the same lie the store exists to prevent.

So the hardening pass did the simplest, most correct thing: throw out my lenient reading and assert the product's own gate.

It went red on the first run. delivered=5003, records=5000, within_bounds=False.

Three records, ambient

The 5,000 test events were all accounted for. The three extras were the daemon's attestation records — the recorder periodically writes "I am the recorder, here's my state" entries into the store it owns. Three of them landed in the store during the soak window.

And the soak wasn't soaking against a store the test owned. It was pointed at the recorder's live store — the real one, with the real daemon writing into it. The delivery count swept up everything the store knew about, which was 5,000 test events plus 3 attestations.

Same class of failure, three times in one hardening week:

Case Looked like Was
FT-STR-2 duplicate deliveries (product bug) soak ran against a shared, ambient store
compliance report nothing written (product bug) --out writes a file; my driver globbed it as a directory
OTel join zero joins (product bug) the fixture is OTel-only — no hook records exist to join

Two of three, the harness. One pattern: the test environment asserting about state it didn't exclusively own.

The fix, and the retraction

The soak now runs against a fresh temp store it creates and owns — no daemon writing into it, no ambient records, nothing in it that the test didn't put there:

delivered=5000, records=5000, within_bounds=True

Deterministic. Re-run, green — for a reason this time.

And the field test log did something I now consider non-negotiable: it recorded the retraction explicitly. The running-fixes log shows FT-STR-2 first as real defect — duplicate deliveries, then reclassified: harness artifact, not a product defect. Both entries stayed in the report. A defect classification is a hypothesis; root cause is allowed to move it; the journal keeps both so the next reader knows how the reasoning went.

tip: if your test asserts a count against shared state, you haven't written a test — you've written a race with extra steps. Count only against state you created.

Why I keep saying the gate was right

The tempting narrative is "false alarm, waste of time." That's the wrong read, and I want to be precise about why.

within_bounds did exactly its job: it flagged a real inconsistency between deliveries and records. The inconsistency was in the test setup — but it was real, it was material, and under the lenient >= reading it had been passing silently the whole time. The strict gate didn't cry wolf. The strict gate found the first wolf available, and the wolf happened to be standing in my own doorway.

If the ambient records had been fewer records instead of more — if the daemon had rewritten or compacted the store mid-soak — the same fence would have caught that too. The gate doesn't know which side the error is on. That's what makes it a gate rather than a cheerleader.

There's a companion piece in the first season of this series — a soak that found a daemon dropping records behind an O(n) lock. Same instrument, opposite direction: that one caught a real product defect, this one caught a test defect. Two soaks, two verdicts, same lesson both times — the soak doesn't tell you where the problem is. It tells you the books don't balance. The classification work after that is yours.

What I keep from this

  1. Soak against a store you own. Shared state isn't realism, it's ambient noise with a deadline attached. A fresh temp store made the test deterministic and meaningful in one move.
  2. Assert the product's own correctness gate, not a laxer reading of it. >= had been passing forever. == failed in ninety seconds. The stricter predicate wasn't harder to write — it was just the one the product actually promises.
  3. Classify before you fix. Product defect vs. harness artifact vs. test-environment contamination are three different work items, and only one of them touches the product. Two of my three reds that week wanted zero product changes.
  4. Retract loudly. The report keeps the wrong classification and the right one, in order. A field test journal that never admits a reclassification is a journal that's editing for optics.

All of it shipped in agentwatch v0.2.1 — on PyPI.

The question worth taking to your own reconciliation tests: what state does your count run against, and did you create all of it? If you can't answer that in one sentence, your next "impossible" failure mode is probably already scheduled.

References

  • Release: agentwatch v0.2.1 on GitHub · on PyPI
  • v0.2.0 field test report — FT-STR-2, the running-fixes log with the reclassification, and the hardening campaign
  • The soak: stream-probe.py — now runs a fresh temp store
  • The product's own gate: within_bounds — exact reconciliation, delivered == records
  • Season 1 companion: the lock-starved daemon — 02 — My Daemon Dropped 1,000 Records and Reported Success
  • Suite: agentic-suite — the full set of agent-security tools

articles.title: JavaScript: The Language That Gaslights Its Developers
articles.description: After writing about PHP's greatest hits in the Weird Language Hall of Fame, it felt only fair to turn...
articles.body_html:
After writing about PHP's greatest hits in the Weird Language Hall of Fame, it felt only fair to turn to JavaScript.

Because if PHP is the language of historical baggage, JavaScript is the language of "this seems impossible, and yet it is fully specified behavior."

JavaScript has a special talent for producing results that look like bugs, feel like bugs, and absolutely are not bugs.

Most of the time, the culprit is type coercion, implicit conversion, or one of the language's many "technically reasonable, emotionally devastating" rules.

So here are a few of my favorite examples.

1. An Empty Array Is Truthy... But Also Equal to false

Let's begin with a classic.

Boolean([])       // true
[] == false       // true
[] === false      // false

This is the kind of thing that makes developers stare at the screen and wonder why they picked computing science instead of accounting like their mom advised.

An empty array is truthy.

So far, so normal:

if ([]) {
  console.log("Yep, truthy");
}

That runs.

But then this also happens:

[] == false   // true

Why?

Because JavaScript doesn't use the same rules for boolean contexts and loose equality.

In a boolean context, arrays are simply objects, and objects are truthy.

But with ==, JavaScript starts converting values. The empty array becomes an empty string, which then becomes the number 0. Meanwhile, false also becomes 0.

So JavaScript ends up comparing:

0 == 0

Which is, unfortunately, true.

And if you really want to ruin your afternoon:

[] == ![]   // true

Because ![] becomes false, and now you're back in the previous example.

The lesson: truthiness and loose equality are not the same thing. If you're comparing values in JavaScript, === should be your default.

2. typeof null Is "object"

This one has survived for decades.

typeof null         // "object"
typeof undefined    // "undefined"
typeof []           // "object"
typeof NaN          // "number"

Let's focus on the weirdest part:

typeof null   // "object"

Except null is not an object.

This is a long-standing historical bug in JavaScript that became untouchable because too much code depended on it.

So now it just lives there, like haunted wallpaper.

And since JavaScript enjoys layering confusion on top of confusion:

  • null is not an object, but typeof null says it is.
  • Arrays are objects, so typeof [] is also "object".
  • NaN means "Not a Number," but typeof NaN is "number".

You can almost hear the language whispering, "If you can't handle me on my worst days, you don't deserve me."

The lesson: typeof is useful, but not always precise. If you need to distinguish arrays, nulls, and objects, use more specific checks like Array.isArray() and explicit value === null.

3. map(parseInt) Produces Nonsense

This is one of the best examples in the entire language because every piece of it looks reasonable.

["10", "10", "10"].map(parseInt)

What would you expect?

[10, 10, 10]

What do you actually get?

[10, NaN, 2]

Naturally.

Here's what's happening.

map() doesn't just pass each array element to the callback. It passes three arguments:

  1. the current value
  2. the current index
  3. the whole array

So this:

["10", "10", "10"].map(parseInt)

effectively becomes:

parseInt("10", 0)  // 10
parseInt("10", 1)  // NaN
parseInt("10", 2)  // 2

And why is that a problem?

Because parseInt() takes a second argument: the radix.

So JavaScript interprets the array index as the number base.

  • "10" in base 0 becomes 10
  • "10" in base 1 is invalid, so NaN
  • "10" in base 2 becomes 2

This is one of those perfect JavaScript moments where two completely legitimate APIs collide and create chaos.

The fix is simple:

["10", "10", "10"].map(Number)

or:

["10", "10", "10"].map(x => parseInt(x, 10))

The lesson: Don't hand a function to map() unless you know exactly what arguments it expects.

4. sort() Sorts Numbers Like Strings

This one has caused real bugs in real applications.

[1, 2, 10, 20, 3].sort()

What you probably expect:

[1, 2, 3, 10, 20]

What JavaScript gives you:

[1, 10, 2, 20, 3]

Because by default, sort() compares elements as strings.

So JavaScript is effectively sorting these:

  • "1"
  • "2"
  • "10"
  • "20"
  • "3"

And in string comparison, "10" comes before "2".

This makes perfect sense if you're sorting words.

It makes much less sense if you're sorting numbers in a programming language and expected numeric order to be the default.

The fix:

[1, 2, 10, 20, 3].sort((a, b) => a - b)

Now you get what you wanted:

[1, 2, 3, 10, 20]

The lesson: JavaScript's default behaviors are often optimized for generality, not for your expectations.

So, Is JavaScript Bad?

Not really.

Like PHP, JavaScript is often mocked for behavior that is actually consistent with its own rules.

The problem is that many of those rules are invisible until you trip over them.

An empty array can be truthy while also loosely equal to false.

typeof null can lie to your face.

A perfectly innocent-looking map(parseInt) can produce results that seem like a prank.

And sort() can rearrange numbers alphabetically, because apparently that was a reasonable default choice at some point in human history.

But that's also what makes JavaScript fascinating.

Its weirdness isn't random. It's the product of a language that was created to validate forms in web pages and became something people use to build microservices and large-scale data streaming pipelines, and evolved while the entire internet was standing on top of it.

Which is kind of impressive.

This is part of a series on programming languages that occasionally make developers question the nature of reality.

PHP already had its turn. Python, C#, and Perl are waiting patiently in the wings.

And Perl, as always, remains less a programming language than a dare.
